submission.title: M-SQE: Multilingual Skill Quality Estimation for Enhancing Language Equality in Agentic Skill Use

findings.title: Abstract's "at least +3.5 points across three different retrievers" fails under its natural per-retriever reading
findings.location: Abstract (p1, lines 24-26); Table 3 (p6)
findings.evidence: "M-SQE's task success exceeds existing baseline's average by at least +3.5 points across three different retrievers." Recomputed per-retriever 3-domain means from Table 3: M-SQE BM25 (74.5+39.6+90.4)/3=68.2, Neural (79.8+36.2+90.4)/3=68.8, SkillFlow-retriever (76.6+40.4+94.2)/3=70.4; strongest baseline (SkillFlow selector) 63.7 / 65.7 / 67.4. Margins: +4.5 / +3.1 / +3.0.
findings.claim: Read distributively ("across three retrievers" = for each retriever), the claim is false: the margin over the strongest baseline is +3.1 (Neural) and +3.0 (SkillFlow retriever), below 3.5 for two of three retrievers. The claim is true only as a single grand average pooled over all 9 settings (69.1 vs 65.6 = +3.5, with zero slack for "at least"; 3.51 unrounded). At the per-setting level it fails outright: two columns are ties (+0.0 at Tool-Neural and Cultural-Neural), and the average margin vs the per-column strongest baseline is +2.9.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the abstract's primary quantitative claim. The precise version the paper can defend (+3.5 grand-average vs one fixed baseline, exactly at the stated bound) is materially weaker than what the sentence communicates, and a careful reader recomputing per retriever will find the stated bound violated.
findings.verifier_note: Every number recomputed and verified from Table 3: M-SQE per-retriever three-domain means 68.17 (BM25), 68.80 (Neural), 70.40 (SkillFlow-retriever) vs strongest baseline SkillFlow's 63.67/65.73/67.43, giving margins +4.5/+3.07/+2.97 — below 3.5 for two of three retrievers; the pooled comparison is 69.12 vs 65.61 = +3.51, exactly the 'at least +3.5' with no slack; the ties (Tool-Neural 36.2 = SkillFlow 36.2; Cultural-Neural 90.4 = mMARCO 90.4) and the +2.87 mean margin vs per-column strongest baseline all check. The strongest rebuttal — Sec 5.5's 'reaching 69.1% average success, +3.5pp over the strongest baseline, SkillFlow (65.6%)' shows the pooled reading was intended — was anticipated by the finding and does not repair the abstract sentence, whose natural distributive reading ('at least +3.5 points across three different retrievers') is false.

findings.title: "Equality" is claimed in title/abstract/contributions but no gap or dispersion metric is ever measured; M-SQE's own per-language numbers show 27-43pp residual spread
findings.location: Title; Abstract (lines 28-30); Sec 1 contribution 2 (lines 122-124); Fig 3 (p6, extraction lines 501-535); Conclusion (p7)
findings.evidence: "thereby moving agentic skill use toward linguistic and cultural equality"; "We demonstrate that M-SQE narrows the language inequality of agentic skill use". Fig 3's extracted M-SQE labels: Tool-Use en 45.8, fr 36.6, hi 54.6, ja 37.4, ko 28.3, sw 41.1, zh 27.2 (spread 27.4pp); General fr 66.7, hi 68.3, ja 87.7, ko 100.0, sw 89.6, zh 56.9 (spread 43.1pp).
findings.claim: Equality/narrowing is a claim about the cross-language gap, but the paper reports no before/after dispersion, variance, min-language, or gap-to-English metric anywhere; the only evidence offered is absolute gains on two languages in one domain. My arithmetic reconciliation (see strengths) confirms the extracted labels are the M-SQE series averaged over three retrievers, so post-M-SQE inequality remains large — Chinese (27.2) and Korean (28.3) sit far below Hindi (54.6) in Tool-Use, and Chinese (56.9) is 43pp below Korean (100.0) in General. The evidence is consistent with inequality being relocated (hi/sw up, zh/ko now lowest) rather than narrowed; whether the overall spread shrank vs Retrieve-only cannot be determined because baseline per-language values are not reported.
findings.why_it_matters: The equality framing is in the paper's title and is the stated social contribution. "Narrows inequality" is verifiable only with a gap metric comparing M-SQE against the baseline across all languages; without it, the demonstrated result is "improves two zero-resource languages," a genuinely valuable but strictly weaker claim.
findings.verifier_note: I independently re-derived the load-bearing attribution: exhaustive integer-feasibility search shows all three Fig 3 panels are impossible as any single-retriever series (minimum per-label denominators sum to 201>94, 436>265, 56>52 tasks) and exactly feasible as M-SQE averaged over three retrievers with totals 217/282, 308/795, 143/156 matching Table 3's implied counts; Retrieve-only-averaged is infeasible for Tool and Cultural, and Random is excluded for Cultural (its 68.2 average lies below the minimum label 86.7). So the labels are M-SQE's, and the quoted post-M-SQE spreads are verified: Tool-Use 54.6 (hi) vs 27.2 (zh) = 27.4pp; General 100.0 (ko) vs 56.9 (zh) = 43.1pp. The full text contains no dispersion, variance, min-language, or gap metric anywhere, and no appendix is cited for per-language baseline values, so this is not an appendix-deferral case; the narrowing claim rests solely on hi/sw absolute deltas that Secs 2/5.5 scope to Tool-Use. The rebuttal that Fig 3's baseline bars are visible in the PDF supplies no computed gap statistic and no reported numbers.

findings.title: The +12.9pp/+5.6pp Hindi/Swahili deltas never state their comparator, the superlative "lifts most" is unverifiable, and the abstract omits that they are Tool-Use-only
findings.location: Abstract (lines 26-28); Sec 1 contribution 2; Sec 2 (lines 147-149); Sec 5.5 (lines 592-599); Fig 3 (p6)
findings.evidence: "M-SQE lifts the lowest-resource languages most (+12.9pp on Hindi and +5.6pp on Swahili)" (Abstract, unscoped); Sec 2 scopes it: "On agentic tool-use tasks... task success rises by +12.9pp on Hindi and +5.6pp on Swahili." Fig 3's legend lists three series (Random, Retrieve-only, M-SQE) but no text states which one the deltas are measured against, nor the retriever aggregation.
findings.claim: (i) No sentence in the paper states whether +12.9/+5.6 is vs Retrieve-only or vs Random. (ii) "Lifts the lowest-resource languages most" requires every other language's lift to be below +5.6pp; the other languages' deltas appear nowhere in text or tables and the baseline bar values did not survive extraction, so the superlative is unverifiable from the provided material. (iii) The abstract and contribution bullet state the deltas without the Tool-Use scoping that Sec 2/5.5 apply; in the General domain, Fig 3's Hindi value (68.3) is second-lowest of six languages, so the unscoped claim is at best domain-specific. This is under-specification of a headline number, not demonstrated falsity.
findings.why_it_matters: These are the paper's equality headline numbers, repeated four times (abstract, contribution, Sec 2, Sec 5.5). A delta without a stated comparator cannot be checked or reproduced, and the unscoped abstract wording invites readers to generalize a Tool-Use-only result to all three domains.
findings.verifier_note: (i) Verified: no sentence in the abstract, Sec 2, or Sec 5.5 names the comparator for +12.9/+5.6, even though the paper names comparators for its other headline deltas ('+6.3pp over Retrieve-only and +14.0pp over Random' — both recomputed correct: 69.12−62.83, 69.12−55.14), and Fig 3's legend lists two baseline series (Random, Retrieve-only), so the anchor is genuinely ambiguous; inferring Retrieve-only from context is plausible but unstated. (ii) Verified: no other language's delta appears anywhere in the provided text, and baseline bar values did not survive extraction, so the superlative 'lifts the lowest-resource languages most' (requiring all other lifts at or below +5.6pp) is unverifiable from the provided material — correctly framed as unverifiable, not false. (iii) Verified: abstract (lines 26-28) and contribution 2 (lines 122-124) state the deltas unscoped, while Sec 2 ('On agentic tool-use tasks') and Sec 5.5 ('Tool Use success rises') establish they are Tool-Use-only. One evidentiary side-step — Hindi's 68.3 being second-lowest absolute in General does not bear on whether its General delta was largest — but the scoping mismatch is established directly from the text, so the finding stands without it.

findings.title: Table 5's "best fine-tuned model" claim rests on a 3-task total margin (out of 411 tasks) with a tie in one of three domains
findings.location: Sec 5 "Downstream Trajectory Generalization" and Table 5 (p7, lines 707-732)
findings.evidence: Table 5: Retrieve-only 36.17 / 12.83 / 50.00; M-SQE 38.30 / 13.21 / 50.00. Prose: "M-SQE yields the best fine-tuned model averagely in three domains (Table 5). The signal that picks better skills to read also picks better skills to learn from, extending M-SQE from an inference-time filter to a beneficial training-data constructor."
findings.claim: Recomputed margins over Retrieve-only: General +2.13pp = 2 tasks (36/94 vs 34/94), Tool-Use +0.38pp = 1 task (35/265 vs 34/265), Cultural 0.00 — an exact tie (26/52 both). Average 33.84 vs 33.00, i.e., +0.84pp = 3 tasks total. The claim "best... averagely" is technically true but the concluding generalization ("picks better skills to learn from", "beneficial training-data constructor") is drawn from a margin of three tasks with no reported variance, seeds, or significance for this experiment in the main text, and a tie in one of the three domains that the prose does not acknowledge.
findings.why_it_matters: This experiment is what elevates M-SQE from a selection method to a training-data method — a distinct contribution claim. Three tasks out of 411 is within plausible single-run fine-tuning noise; the wording claims a capability the table's own margins do not establish.
findings.verifier_note: All integer reconstructions verified: General 36.17=34/94 vs 38.30=36/94 (+2 tasks); Tool-Use 12.83=34/265 vs 13.21=35/265 (+1 task); Cultural 50.00=26/52 for both (exact tie, unmentioned in prose); averages 33.84 vs 33.00 = +0.84pp = 3 net tasks. Prose quoted verbatim (lines 728-732). Rebuttals tested and defeated: 'averagely' hedges the best-on-average claim but the prose never discloses the tie or the one-task Tool margin; the Sec 5.5 pointer 'significance analyses are in Appendix B' sits in the Table 3 Main Results paragraph and the finding correctly scopes its charge to the main text; and the larger margin vs Random (+3.65pp, 9 tasks) does not rescue the specific generalization that M-SQE's signal 'picks better skills to learn from' than retrieval ranking, where the margin is 3 tasks with a domain tie.

findings.title: Sec 2's claim that region-consistency "is the evidence" of cultural correctness over surface fluency is not licensed by the design, and rests on tiny per-region samples with an unstated comparator
findings.location: Sec 2 (p2, lines 159-165); Fig 3 Cultural panel (p6); Table 2 (p5)
findings.evidence: "M-SQE's cultural gains hold with stable deltas across six main culture regions... with strong gains in South Asia (+6.6pp) and Oceania (+8.4pp). This region-by-region consistency, not a single number, is the evidence that M-SQE's quality signal captures cultural correctness rather than surface fluency." Table 2: the Cultural domain has 52 tasks total across six regions.
findings.claim: Sec 2's claim that 'region-by-region consistency... is the evidence that M-SQE's quality signal captures cultural correctness rather than surface fluency' is not licensed by the evidence cited: a selector preferring better-translated skills would also yield region-consistent gains on a correctness checker whenever fluency correlates with correctness, and the analyses that could discriminate the mechanism (error typology, case studies) are deferred to Appendix I and unverifiable from the provided material. The statistical basis is also thin and unreportable: 52 cultural tasks across six regions (mean ~8.7 per region, per-region counts nowhere stated) mean each regional delta rests on a handful of net tasks. Finally, the +6.6/+8.4 deltas name no comparator, and if the comparator is any count-based series the printed values can only arise from subtracting independently rounded endpoints (the underlying grid differences round to 6.7 and 8.3).
findings.why_it_matters: This is the central evidentiary claim of the mandatory social-impact section, and it explicitly asserts an evidential relationship ("is the evidence that") the experimental design cannot support: no analysis in the provided material separates cultural-fact errors from fluency errors.
findings.verifier_note: Part (i) survives: the Sec 2 sentence (quoted accurately, lines 159-165) asserts a mechanism ('captures cultural correctness rather than surface fluency') that region-consistent gains on a correctness checker cannot discriminate — a fluency-correlated selector would produce the same pattern if fluency proxies correctness in the pool — and the discriminating analyses are deferred to Appendix I (unverifiable, not missing). But (ii) overreaches: my exhaustive enumeration of Fig 3-consistent region-size assignments shows feasible sizes span 1-36 (the 86.7 region is in {5,10,15,20,25}; the 91.7 regions are multiples of 4 up to 36), so 'roughly 4-15 tasks per region' is not established and 'about one net task' holds only in the minimal-size case (South Asia's +6.6pp is 1-5 net tasks over three runs depending on size). And (iii) is not forced: the rounded-endpoint forensic (6.6 vs true 6.7; 8.4 vs true 8.3) is valid only if the comparator is a count-grid series like Retrieve-only; since the comparator is unstated — as the finding itself asserts — a seed-averaged Random comparator could yield an unrounded delta printing +6.6, so 'deltas computed from rounded numbers' is plausible but unproven.

findings.title: Fig 3 never states what it aggregates; its labels are provably not a single-retriever series and can only be three-retriever averages
findings.location: Fig 3 and caption (p6, lines 501-538); Sec 5.5 "Robustness across Regions and Languages"
findings.evidence: Caption: "Success rate across culture regions and languages" — no retriever or aggregation stated. Cultural labels 86.7, 93.3, 91.7, 100.0, 100.0, 91.7 over 52 tasks: under any single retriever, 86.7 forces a >=15-task region (13/15), 93.3 another >=15, and each 91.7 a >=12-task region, requiring >=54 > 52 tasks — impossible. Exhaustive search confirms all three panels are infeasible as any single-retriever series but exactly feasible as M-SQE averaged over the three retrievers (totals 217/282, 308/795, 143/156 matching Table 3's implied counts).
findings.claim: Fig 3's aggregation basis (mean over BM25/Neural/SkillFlow) is stated nowhere in the caption or text and is recoverable only by forensic arithmetic — the labels are integer-infeasible as any single-retriever series yet reconcile exactly with Table 3 as M-SQE averaged over the three retrievers. Per-language and per-region task counts are also unreported in the main text; with 52 cultural tasks over six regions the regional bars necessarily rest on small samples (feasible sizes range from 1 to a few dozen), which readers cannot assess. Under-specification, not error — the numbers themselves reconcile with Table 3 once the reading is inferred.
findings.why_it_matters: Fig 3 carries the paper's equality evidence; without the aggregation basis and per-group Ns, none of its bars or the deltas quoted from it can be checked or reproduced by a reader.
findings.verifier_note: The core is fully verified: the caption and Sec 5.5 state no retriever or aggregation basis; Table 2 reports no per-language or per-region task counts; and I independently reproduced the exhaustive search — all three panels are integer-infeasible as any single-retriever series (Cultural: 86.7 forces a >=15-task region, 93.3 another >=15, each 91.7 a >=12-task region, total >=54 > 52, exactly as claimed; General needs 201>94; Tool needs 436>265) and exactly feasible as M-SQE averaged over three retrievers with totals 217/282, 308/795, 143/156 matching Table 3. One clause overreaches: 'regional bars rest on roughly 4-15 tasks each' is not established — my enumeration of all 223 feasible Cultural assignments shows region sizes from 1 to 36 (the two 100.0 regions can be as small as 1-2), so a rebuttal disclosing an actual region of 16+ or 1-3 tasks would falsify that specific range.

findings.title: Two of six Fig 6 delta labels do not match their own printed endpoints
findings.location: Fig 6 (p7, extraction lines 679-702)
findings.claim: Two of Fig 6's six printed deltas differ by 0.1pp from the difference of their printed endpoints ('57.0 / 64.1 / +7.0 pp' vs recomputed 7.1; '53.6 / 58.5 / +5.0 pp' vs recomputed 4.9), while the other four check exactly. This is most plausibly benign (deltas computed from unrounded values, endpoints rounded separately), but as printed the figure is internally inconsistent and should be regenerated with a consistent rounding rule. Sec 5.5's '+3.5-9.0pp' range is unaffected, since both of its endpoints come from cells that check exactly.
findings.why_it_matters: Small, but it signals inconsistent rounding practice across the paper's reported deltas (the same rounded-endpoint-subtraction pattern appears in Sec 2's +6.6/+8.4), which slightly undermines confidence in every delta not recomputable from a table.
findings.verifier_note: The core arithmetic is confirmed: 64.1−57.0 = 7.1 vs printed '+7.0 pp' and 58.5−53.6 = 4.9 vs printed '+5.0 pp', while the other four cells check exactly (8.6, 9.0, 6.4, 3.5), and the triple groupings are unambiguous in the extraction (each Retrieve-only/M-SQE/delta triple is adjacent and the four exact cells confirm the pattern). The benign explanation also checks: unrounded three-domain averages admit endpoint/delta pairs consistent with both printings. But the final clause overreaches: the text's '+3.5-9.0pp above Retrieve-only' range does NOT inherit the inconsistency — both endpoints come from cells that check exactly (61.4−57.9=3.5; 66.0−57.0=9.0), and the recomputed six deltas (8.6, 9.0, 6.4, 7.1, 3.5, 4.9) span the identical 3.5-9.0 range, so the textual claim is unaffected either way.

findings.title: Several verified headline wins are 1-2 task margins or ties, and the significance analysis backing them is in unprovided Appendix B
findings.location: Table 3 (p6); Sec 5.5 ("significance analyses are in Appendix B"); Fig 3-5 baseline series
findings.evidence: Cultural-SF: 94.2 vs 92.3 = 1 task (49/52 vs 48/52); Cultural-Neural: 90.4 vs mMARCO 90.4 — tie; Tool-Neural: 36.2 vs SkillFlow 36.2 — tie; General-SF: 76.6 vs 74.5 = 2 tasks. The Cultural domain has 52 tasks in total.
findings.claim: The claim "first or tied-first... in all 9 settings" is accurate (verified below), but with 52-94 tasks per domain, several per-column wins are within one or two tasks and two are exact ties. Whether these margins are significant is deferred to Appendix B, which is not in the provided material — as are the other load-bearing supports that cannot be checked here: baseline series values behind "matches or exceeds both baselines in every breakdown" (Fig 3 caption) and Figs 4-5's quoted margins (+3.4/+9.7, +8.1/+4.5), the audit protocol behind Table 1 (App A), parameter-perturbation stability (App C), and leakage control (App E). These are unverifiable-from-provided-material, not evidence of bad faith — the paper gives a concrete supplementary pointer (footnote 1).
findings.why_it_matters: The reviewer-checkable record supports the direction of every claim but not the robustness of the closest ones; the paper's defense of its 1-task cultural margins rests entirely on material a reader of the main text cannot see.
findings.verifier_note: Every element verified. 'First or tied-first in all 9 settings' checked column by column against Table 3 (seven strict wins, two ties). The task-count reconstructions are exact: Cultural-SF 94.2=49/52 vs 92.3=48/52 (one task); Cultural-Neural 90.4 = mMARCO 90.4 (tie); Tool-Neural 36.2 = SkillFlow 36.2 (tie); General-SF 76.6=72/94 vs SkillFlow 74.5=70/94 (two tasks). Every deferral cited is real and correctly named: significance to Appendix B (line 585-586), audit protocol to Appendix A (line 67), parameter perturbation to Appendix C (line 359), leakage control to Appendix E (lines 380/469); Figs 4-5's quoted margins (+3.4/+9.7 at line 656, +8.1/+4.5 at lines 668-669) and Fig 3's caption claim indeed have no recoverable baseline values in the extraction. The finding correctly frames all of this as unverifiable-from-provided-material rather than missing, and credits the concrete supplementary pointer (footnote 1) — exactly the calibration the process facts require. Minor imprecision only: '52-94 tasks per domain' elides Tool-Use's 265, but all cited thin margins are in the 52- and 94-task domains, so nothing load-bearing changes.

findings.title: Fig. 3 per-breakdown success rates are arithmetically impossible as single-retriever rates over the stated task counts; an undisclosed aggregation (retriever pooling) must be involved
findings.location: Fig. 3 (p.6, extracted labels lines 501-535) vs Table 2 (p.5: 94 General / 265 Tool / 52 Cultural tasks)
findings.evidence: Cultural panel labels: "86.7 / 93.3 91.7 / 100.0 100.0 / 91.7" over "Six main cultural regions" with Table 2 stating 52 tasks. General panel labels: "66.7 68.3 87.7 100.0 89.6 56.9" over six languages with 94 tasks. Caption: "Success rate across culture regions and languages" — no retriever or aggregation is stated.
findings.claim: Assuming one label per region, the minimum denominators that can produce these values are 86.7->n>=15 (13/15), 93.3->n>=15 (14/15), 91.7->n>=12 (11/12, twice), so the six regions need at least 15+15+12+12+1+1 = 56 tasks > 52; no partition of 52 tasks works at single-retriever resolution. The same holds for the General panel: 68.3 requires n>=41 (28/41) and 87.7 requires n>=57 (50/57), and 41+57 = 98 > 94 already. The values DO reconcile exactly if each bar pools successes across the three retrievers (denominator 3*n_region): e.g., region counts (20,5,8,6,5,8) give 52/60=86.7, 14/15=93.3, 22/24=91.7, 18/18=100, 15/15=100, 22/24=91.7, totaling 143 successes over 156 trials = 91.67%, exactly matching Table 3's M-SQE cultural cells (47+47+49)/156. But neither the pooling nor the per-region/per-language counts are stated anywhere in the paper. (Caveat per extraction: series attribution of bar labels is ambiguous, but the minimum-denominator argument is series-independent since regions share denominators; the reconciliation with Table 3 additionally supports the labels being M-SQE bars.)
findings.why_it_matters: Fig. 3 is the paper's central equality evidence (cited in the abstract, Sec. 2, and Sec. 5.5). As printed, its y-axis quantity cannot be what the caption implies. Under every reconstruction that works, several regions are backed by only ~4-8 tasks, which the reader cannot know because per-breakdown n is never disclosed. The authors should state Fig. 3's aggregation rule and per-region/per-language task counts explicitly.
findings.verifier_note: All arithmetic verified: minimum denominators for 86.7 (13/15), 93.3 (14/15), and 91.7 twice (11/12) sum to 56>52 cultural tasks, and I scanned all smaller n to confirm the minima; for the General panel 68.3 needs n>=41 (28/41) and 87.7 needs n>=57 (50/57), 98>94. The 3-retriever pooling reconstruction with region sizes (20,5,8,6,5,8) reproduces all six labels exactly and totals 143/156=91.67%, exactly matching Table 3's M-SQE cultural cells (47+47+49)/156; I additionally found a General-panel partition (12,20,19,10,16,17) whose pooled successes equal exactly (70+75+72)/282, further corroborating pooling. The impossibility is robust to rounding convention (truncation makes it worse). The one-label-per-region attribution is effectively forced: every panel's label count equals its category count (6 labels/6 regions, 6/6 languages, 7/7 languages), so the labels are one series (evidently M-SQE). Neither the Fig. 3 caption ('Success rate across culture regions and languages') nor Sec. 5.5 states any aggregation, and Table 2 gives no per-region or per-language counts. A rebuttal can only supply the missing aggregation statement, which confirms rather than dissolves the finding.

findings.title: The Sec. 2 per-region 'strong gains' (+6.6pp South Asia, +8.4pp Oceania) correspond to 1-2 task successes and sit off every achievable exact grid
findings.location: Sec. 2 'Social Impact', p.2 (lines 160-165), with Fig. 3 (p.6) and Table 2 (52 cultural tasks)
findings.evidence: "matching or exceeding both baselines in every region, with strong gains in South Asia (+6.6pp) and Oceania (+8.4pp). This region-by-region consistency, not a single number, is the evidence that M-SQE's quality signal captures cultural correctness"
findings.claim: The Social Impact section's headline regional gains (+6.6pp South Asia, +8.4pp Oceania) rest on regions of roughly 5-8 tasks each (52 tasks over six regions; ~11.5pp per task at single-retriever resolution), so each delta corresponds to about one-to-two task successes at best; neither value is expressible as an exact task-count difference d/n or d/(3n) for any region size compatible with 52 tasks, consistent with subtraction of independently rounded Fig. 3 bar values (93.3-86.7=6.6 where the exact grid difference 1/15 rounds to 6.7) or with comparison against an averaged Random baseline; and the comparison baseline for these deltas is never stated. On sample sizes this small, region-level deltas cannot support the section's claim that 'region-by-region consistency... is the evidence' of cultural correctness.
findings.why_it_matters: The social-impact section's cultural-equality argument explicitly rests on 'region-by-region consistency' — but at n≈5-10 tasks per region, per-region deltas of 1-2 successes are statistically meaningless, and the ±0.1pp rounding errors show the numbers were not computed from the underlying counts. This is the kind of claim a skeptical reader will discount entirely unless per-region n and the aggregation are disclosed.
findings.verifier_note: The core is verified: 52 tasks over six regions means ~8.7 tasks/region (~11.5pp per task at single-retriever resolution); by exhaustive scan neither 6.6 nor 8.4 is expressible as d/n or d/(3n) for any region size compatible with 52 tasks (3n<=156); 93.3-86.7=6.6 and 91.7-83.3=8.4 match subtraction of rounded values whose exact grid differences (1/15=6.67, 2/24=8.33) round to 6.7 and 8.3; and Sec. 2 never states the comparison baseline ('matching or exceeding both baselines... with strong gains in South Asia (+6.6pp) and Oceania (+8.4pp)'). But two sub-claims overreach: (1) 'indicating the deltas were computed from rounded numbers' and (2) 'on every reconstruction consistent with Fig. 3, the South Asia gain is exactly one additional task success'. The unstated baseline could be the Random row, which the paper's own Table 3 shows is an off-grid average (60.0, 79.2 are not k/52), so an exact non-grid delta vs an averaged Random baseline is a live alternative; the baseline bars' values did not survive extraction, so 86.7/83.3 as the specific baseline endpoints is a plausible hypothesis, not forced. Either way the magnitude is ~one pooled task success (6.6% of 15 pooled trials = 0.99), so the substance survives.

findings.title: In 5 of 9 settings the margin over the strongest baseline is 1-5 tasks (plus 2 exact ties); at most one, possibly two, per-cell wins could survive a paired significance test
findings.location: Table 3 and Sec. 5.5 'Main Results' (p.6)
findings.evidence: "Table 3 shows M-SQE first or tied-first against the single strongest baseline in all 9 domain-by-retriever settings, reaching 69.1% average success, +3.5pp over the strongest baseline, SkillFlow (65.6%); significance analyses are in Appendix B." Recomputed margins in task counts: General 70-67=+3, 75-70=+5, 72-70=+2 (n=94); Tool-Use 105-88=+17, 96-96=0 (tie with SkillFlow at 36.2), 107-99=+8 (n=265); Cultural 47-45=+2, 47-47=0 (tie with mMARCO at 90.4), 49-48=+1 (n=52).
findings.claim: Only Tool-Use/BM25 (+17/265) plausibly survives a per-cell paired test. Even in the theoretical best case of fully one-sided discordance, +5/94 gives exact two-sided p=0.0625, +8/265 gives p=0.008 only if all discordants favor M-SQE (realistic discordance pushes it to p~0.2-0.3), and +1 or +2 of 52 can never reach p<0.05. The two exact ties are covered only by the generic phrase 'first or tied-first' and never individually acknowledged. Moreover the 9 settings reuse the same 411 tasks across the three retrievers, so they are correlated repetitions, not nine independent confirmations. Appendix B is unverifiable from the provided material; to accept the per-setting superiority claim I would need App B to report paired per-cell tests (e.g., McNemar) and a task-level aggregate test — the printed margins already guarantee that most per-cell comparisons cannot individually be significant regardless of App B's method. (For fairness: the anchors comparison is much stronger — vs Retrieve-only the Tool-Use margins are +29 and +28 tasks of 265, which would clearly survive testing, so the +6.3pp anchor claim is on firmer ground than the +3.5pp strongest-baseline claim.)
findings.why_it_matters: The headline framing ('first or tied-first in all 9 settings') is literally accurate but derives most of its rhetorical force from cells whose margins are 1-5 tasks of shared, correlated task sets. The defensible claim is aggregate superiority plus one strong cell, not nine wins.
findings.verifier_note: Every recomputed margin checks out against Table 3: General +3 (70-67/94), +5 (75-70/94), +2 (72-70/94); Tool-Use +17 (105-88/265), tie (96/265 vs SkillFlow 36.2), +8 (107-99/265); Cultural +2 (47-45/52), tie (47/52 vs mMARCO 90.4), +1 (49-48/52). The exact sign-test bounds are correct: b=5,c=0 gives p=0.0625; b=8,c=0 gives p=0.0078; margins of +1 or +2 can never reach p<0.05 under any paired test. The 9 settings do reuse the same 411 tasks across three retrievers, so they are three correlated repetitions per domain, not nine independent confirmations. The ties are covered only by 'first or tied-first' (Sec. 5.5) and never individually flagged. I tried the rebuttal 'the paper never claims per-cell significance; App B has the tests' — but the finding already frames App B as unverifiable-not-missing and correctly states what App B would need to show, and the arithmetic fact that most cells cannot individually be significant at the printed margins is rebuttal-proof. The finding also fairly concedes the Retrieve-only anchor (+29 and +28 of 265, verified: 105-76, 96-68) is robust. Its only soft spot — 'realistic discordance pushes +8/265 to p~0.2-0.3' assumes fairly high discordance (moderate discordance gives p~0.04-0.12) — is hedged with 'plausibly' and does not affect the core.

findings.title: The trajectory-generalization claim (Table 5) rests on a net margin of 3 task successes out of 411, including an unacknowledged tie
findings.location: Table 5 and Sec. 5.5 'Downstream Trajectory Generalization' (p.7, lines 707-732)
findings.evidence: Table 5: Retrieve-only 36.17 / 12.83 / 50.00 vs M-SQE 38.30 / 13.21 / 50.00. Text: "M-SQE yields the best fine-tuned model averagely in three domains (Table 5). The signal that picks better skills to read also picks better skills to learn from."
findings.claim: All 12 cells are exactly integer-consistent (verified: 34/94, 32/265, 22/52, etc.), so the margins are exact: General 36 vs 34 of 94 (+2 tasks), Tool-Use 35 vs 34 of 265 (+1 task), Cultural 26 vs 26 of 52 (exact tie, not mentioned in the prose). Net advantage over Retrieve-only: +3 tasks of 411, i.e. +0.84pp on the three-domain average, in a single fine-tuning run with no variance estimate. The direction is consistent (>= in all three domains), but the stated conclusion — that M-SQE extends to 'a beneficial training-data constructor' — is at noise level on this evidence.
findings.why_it_matters: This is presented as a contribution-extending result ('extending M-SQE from an inference-time filter to a beneficial training-data constructor'), yet a single task flipping in either domain would erase or reverse it. It should be presented as suggestive at best, with the Cultural tie stated.
findings.verifier_note: All 12 Table 5 cells verified integer-consistent (36.17=34/94, 38.30=36/94, 35.11=33/94; 12.08=32/265, 12.83=34/265, 10.19=27/265, 13.21=35/265; 42.31=22/52, 50.00=26/52 twice, 38.46=20/52), which both fixes the margins exactly (General +2, Tool-Use +1, Cultural exact tie 26/52=26/52) and implies a single run — multi-seed averaging landing on exact k/n in all 12 cells is not credible. Net +3 tasks of 411; three-domain averages 33.84 vs 33.00 = +0.84pp, as claimed. The prose ('M-SQE yields the best fine-tuned model averagely in three domains... extending M-SQE... to a beneficial training-data constructor') does not mention the Cultural tie and reports no variance. The only available rebuttal — directional consistency across domains — is already conceded in the finding. The literal claim 'best... averagely' is true, but the finding attacks evidential weight, not literal truth, and +3/411 in one run cannot support the generalization conclusion.

findings.title: The Random baseline is averaged over an unstated number of draws, and no other row carries any variance information
findings.location: Table 3, 'Random' row (p.6); Sec. 5.3 (p.5) defines Random only as "a uniform selection from the candidate set"
findings.evidence: Random cells 66.2 and 70.6 (n=94), 26.1, 26.6, 33.1 (n=265), and 60.0, 79.2 (n=52) are not expressible as k/n for any integer k (e.g., on n=94 the neighbors of 66.2 are 62/94=66.0 and 63/94=67.0; on n=52 the neighbors of 60.0 are 59.6 and 61.5). Every cell of every other row IS exactly k/n.
findings.claim: The Random row must be an average over multiple random draws, but the number of draws/seeds is nowhere stated in the main text; conversely, the integer-exactness of all other rows implies every deterministic method (and the LLM scorer/solver pipeline) is reported from a single run with no seed variance or confidence interval anywhere in Table 3/4/5. Solver decoding settings are deferred to Appendix F (unverifiable from the provided material).
findings.why_it_matters: Under-specified aggregation for one baseline and single-run point estimates for everything else make it impossible to judge run-to-run noise against the 1-5 task margins discussed above.
findings.verifier_note: Verified both halves. The seven cited Random cells are all off-grid (66.2 and 70.6 on n=94: neighbors 62/94=66.0, 63/94=67.0, 66/94=70.2, 67/94=71.3; 26.1, 26.6, 33.1 on n=265: neighbors 26.0/26.4, 26.4/26.8, 32.8/33.2; 60.0 and 79.2 on n=52: neighbors 59.6/61.5 and 78.8/80.8) — and the finding correctly excluded the two Random cells that ARE expressible (69.1=65/94, 65.4=34/52), showing care. I spot-checked every cell of all eight other Table 3 rows and all 12 Table 5 cells: each is exactly k/n on its domain size. Sec. 5.3 defines Random only as 'a uniform selection from the candidate set' with no draw count; no seed variance or CI appears anywhere in Tables 3/4/5; solver decoding is deferred to Appendix F (properly treated as unverifiable, not missing). The rebuttal 'the LLM pipeline is deterministic under greedy decoding' would justify single-run reporting but not the absence of any statement to that effect, and does not explain the Random row's aggregation. Correctly scoped as minor.

findings.title: The abstract's 'at least +3.5 points across three different retrievers' does not hold at the per-retriever level
findings.location: Abstract (p.1, lines 24-26)
findings.evidence: "M-SQE's task success exceeds existing baseline's average by at least +3.5 points across three different retrievers." Recomputed per-retriever three-domain averages vs SkillFlow (strongest baseline): BM25 68.17 vs 63.67 (+4.5), Neural 68.80 vs 65.73 (+3.1), SkillFlow-retriever 70.40 vs 67.43 (+3.0).
findings.claim: 'At least +3.5' is true only for the pooled 9-cell average (69.12 vs 65.61 = +3.51). Under the natural reading of 'across three different retrievers' — that the margin holds for each retriever — it is false for two of the three retrievers (+3.1 and +3.0).
findings.why_it_matters: A precise headline number in the abstract should survive its most natural reading; as phrased it overstates the per-retriever result by up to 0.5pp.
findings.verifier_note: All recomputations verified from Table 3: pooled 9-cell averages 69.12 (M-SQE) vs 65.61 (SkillFlow) = +3.51, so '+3.5' binds only in the pooled reading and only barely; per-retriever three-domain averages vs SkillFlow are BM25 68.17-63.67=+4.5, Neural 68.80-65.73=+3.07, SkillFlow-retriever 70.40-67.43=+2.97. I attempted the strongest rebuttal — that 'at least +3.5' ranges over baselines (minimum being vs SkillFlow) with 'across three different retrievers' merely describing the evaluation scope, supported by the body text '+3.5pp over the strongest baseline, SkillFlow (65.6%)'. That reading makes the sentence literally defensible, but the finding is stated conditionally ('under the natural reading') and both of its factual assertions are true: the bound holds only for the pooled average, and it fails for two of three retrievers read distributively. A distributive reading of 'at least X across Y' is at minimum a live default reading, so the sentence misleads as phrased; a rebuttal can fix the wording but not deny the per-retriever numbers. Correctly scoped as minor.

findings.title: The candidate-depth rule K = 10*floor(|S|/1000) is degenerate for pools under 1,000 skills and reads as a post-hoc fit to the three pool sizes
findings.location: Sec. 5.3 (p.5, line 479) and Table 2 (p.5); Fig. 4 (p.7)
findings.evidence: "Retriever candidate depth follows K = 10 · ⌊|S|/1000⌋"; Table 2: pool sizes 1,750 / 2,299 / 5,285 with depths 10 / 20 / 50.
findings.claim: The rule reproduces all three depths (verified: floor(1.75)=1->10, floor(2.299)=2->20, floor(5.285)=5->50), but it yields K=0 (no candidates at all) for any pool under 1,000 skills and jumps discontinuously (999->0, 1000->10), so it cannot be the general design principle the surrounding trade-off prose presents it as. Presented as a rule it is justified by exactly the three points it was fitted to. Relatedly, for the General domain K=10 equals the largest budget in Fig. 4, so at Top-10 M-SQE's General selection is vacuous (it selects all 10 candidates); the reported narrowing to '+3.4pp at Top10' is therefore partly mechanical, with the Top-10 margin carried entirely by the other two domains.
findings.why_it_matters: A depth formula that returns zero candidates for most realistic small pools signals a description of choices, not a transferable rule; and the budget-sensitivity trend at its right endpoint is partially an artifact of K=N.
findings.verifier_note: Verified: K=10*floor(|S|/1000) reproduces exactly the three Table 2 settings (floor(1.750)=1 gives 10, floor(2.299)=2 gives 20, floor(5.285)=5 gives 50), yields K=0 for any pool under 1,000 skills, and jumps 999 to 0 vs 1,000 to 10 — so the general trade-off rationale in Sec. 5.3 ('too shallow confounds selection quality with retrieval recall... too deep inflates scoring cost') cannot be carried by this formula outside the three pool sizes it matches. Also verified the vacuity point: General candidate depth K=10 equals the largest Fig. 4 budget N=10, so at Top-10 any selector returns all 10 candidates and the General cell contributes zero margin mechanically; the quoted '+3.4pp at Top10' (Sec. 5.5) is therefore carried entirely by Tool-Use (K=20) and Cultural (K=50), and part of the widening-margin narrative at Top-10 is by construction. The rebuttal 'the formula is shorthand for roughly 1% of the pool with a sensible minimum' concedes the printed rule is not the design principle as stated. Correctly scoped as minor.

findings.title: Router evaluation (98.5%) is under-specified: n and label provenance unstated, evaluated in-sample on the routed queries, and 'flipped' is undefined for a 3-class label
findings.location: Sec. 4.4 'Domain Router' (p.4, lines 296-307) and Fig. 5 (p.7)
findings.evidence: "reaching 98.5% accuracy on our three-domain query set. A noise analysis shows the router's labels can be randomly flipped on up to 90% of queries while M-SQE stays ahead of Retrieve-only throughout"; Fig. 5 caption: "1,000 seeds per rate; shaded band = empirical 95% interval); the star marks the 5-shot router used in the main experiments with 1.5% error rate."
findings.claim: The 98.5% router accuracy is reported without n, label provenance, or protocol in the main text; it is numerically consistent with in-sample scoring on the full 411-query evaluation set (405/411, matching Fig. 5's 1.5%-error star), in which case it is an operational sanity check against labels that follow from each task's source benchmark rather than generalization evidence — which of these it is cannot be determined from the provided material (Appendix F). The noise-sweep flip operation is undefined for three classes. Separately, the +4.5pp survival at 90% corruption is expected rather than remarkable: all three fusion rules weight the Action score heavily, and Table 4 shows Action-only alone beats Retrieve-only by +6.5pp with no routing, a point the paper itself concedes.
findings.why_it_matters: The corruption sweep is a genuinely good robustness probe, but the headline 98.5% carries less content than it appears to, and the sweep's flip semantics must be specified for the 1,000-seed experiment to be reproducible.
findings.verifier_note: The verifiable parts hold: the main text (Sec. 4.4) reports '98.5% accuracy on our three-domain query set' with no n and no statement of the label source or protocol; 405/411=98.54% and 6/411=1.46% are consistent with the Fig. 5 star's '1.5% error rate'; 'randomly flipped' is operationally undefined for three classes in the main text; and the robustness arithmetic is verified — Table 4 Action-only (BM25 three-domain average (71.3+38.5+88.5)/3=66.1) already beats Retrieve-only (59.6) by +6.5pp with no routing at all, and the paper concedes 'routing sharpens the margin, and the two views hold the floor'. But the finding overreaches in asserting the in-sample scoring as established ('implying the router is scored on the very queries it routes'): 98.5% at one decimal is consistent with other denominators (e.g., 197/200), so the attribution is plausible but not forced; and even if in-sample, accuracy on the queries the router actually routes is the operationally relevant quantity for the main results — the paper does not claim router generalization beyond its unevidenced 'a new specialized domain can be added the same way' aside. Implementation details are deferred to Appendix F (unverifiable, not missing).

findings.title: Two of six Fig. 6 deltas contradict their own printed endpoints by 0.1pp
findings.location: Fig. 6 (p.7, extracted lines 679-702)
findings.claim: The printed deltas were evidently computed from unrounded values and then rounded independently of the rounded endpoints, so as printed, two cells of the backbone-robustness grid are internally inconsistent. The '+3.5-9.0pp' range quoted in the text does match the six printed deltas.
findings.why_it_matters: Trivially fixable, but in a figure whose entire purpose is quantitative comparison, delta and endpoints should be mutually consistent; it also confirms rounding discipline is applied inconsistently across the paper (cf. the +6.6/+8.4 issue, which errs in the opposite direction by subtracting rounded values).
findings.verifier_note: Verified against the extracted Fig. 6 triples, whose (Retrieve-only, M-SQE, delta) pairing is forced by the contiguous layout under the 'Retrieve-only M-SQE' column headers: 64.1-57.0=7.1 vs printed '+7.0 pp', and 58.5-53.6=4.9 vs printed '+5.0 pp' — two internally inconsistent cells as printed. The other four check exactly (68.2-59.6=8.6, 66.0-57.0=9.0, 65.9-59.5=6.4, 61.4-57.9=3.5), and the text's '+3.5-9.0pp' range matches the six printed deltas. The obvious rebuttal — deltas computed from unrounded values then rounded independently — is already the finding's own stated explanation; it explains the inconsistency but cannot dissolve the fact that the printed grid is internally inconsistent in two cells. Correctly scoped as a minor presentational defect.

findings.title: Table 1's audit sums correctly (~84,680 vs '~84,700') but the main text gives no method caveats for 'Est.' counts, the exact-zero claims, or cross-index double counting
findings.location: Table 1 and Sec. 1 (p.1, lines 40-59)
findings.evidence: 79,700 + 4,000 + 700 + 200 + 80 + 0 + 0 = 84,680, consistent with "∼84,700 audited community skill entries". Method description in main text: "our audit spanning over a dozen public community skill indexes (∼84,700 entries in total, including a popular 38.2k-star skill repository)" and "(full audit protocol in Appendix A)".
findings.claim: The per-language sum checks out, but the main text's only caveats are the 'Est.' column header and tildes. Two things need App A (unverifiable from the provided material) to assess: (1) the exact '0' for Swahili and Hindi is a claim an estimation procedure can only support with a stated detection recall — a language-ID pass with even 1% miss rate cannot certify exact zero across ~84,700 entries; (2) 'over a dozen public indexes' including a starred GitHub repo alongside Hugging Face dataset mirrors invites double counting of the same skill bodies in the ~84,700 total. This is under-specification in the main text, not evidence of error — the paper does provide a concrete pointer (Appendix A in supplementary).
findings.why_it_matters: The zero-supply claim for sw/hi is the motivating fact of the whole paper (repeated in the abstract, Sec. 1, Sec. 2, and Sec. 5.5); the strength of 'zero' versus 'we detected none' depends entirely on audit recall, which a reviewer needs App A to judge.
findings.verifier_note: Verified: the Table 1 column sums to 79,700+4,000+700+200+80+0+0=84,680, consistent with the stated '~84,700 audited community skill entries' — a strength the finding correctly records. The main-text caveats are indeed limited to 'Est.'/'Estimated' and tildes on the nonzero rows, while the prose asserts flat zeros ('Swahili and Hindi... have zero target-language skill content of their own'; the abstract says 'no in-language skill content'; Sec. 5.5 says Table 1 'measures at zero'). Both methodological concerns are sound: certifying an exact 0 across ~84,700 entries requires a stated detection-recall for the language-ID/audit procedure, and aggregating 'over a dozen public community skill indexes' including a 38.2k-star GitHub repository alongside Hugging Face dataset mirrors (LittleDinoC 2026; huzey 2026; wshobson 2026) invites double counting of the same skill bodies in the total. The finding already applies the correct calibration — this is main-text under-specification with a concrete pointer to Appendix A (unverifiable from the provided material), not evidence of error — so no rebuttal short of producing Appendix A itself changes its status, and producing it is exactly what the finding requests.

findings.title: No rubric-free LLM-rerank baseline; Action-only already captures nearly all of the gain, leaving the novel machinery's contribution at 7 tasks of 411
findings.location: Sec 5.3 (p.5, baselines list), Table 4 (p.6), Table 3 (p.6, BM25 columns)
findings.evidence: Table 4 (BM25, Top3): "Theory-only 67.0 28.7 59.6 / Action-only 71.3 38.5 88.5 / M-SQE 74.5 39.6 90.4"; Table 3 Retrieve-only (BM25): 71.3 / 28.7 / 78.8. Baselines are "ToolRerank... SkillFlow('s) own ranking stage... mMARCO... DEITA... M-DaQ... JQL" — none is an LLM prompted to score candidates.
findings.claim: M-SQE is Gemini-3-Flash prompted with a rubric, yet no baseline is a plain LLM prompted to rerank the same candidates, so 'the two-view rubric helps' cannot be distinguished from 'any strong LLM judging candidates helps'. The closest proxy is Table 4's Action-only (query-conditioned single-view LLM scoring, still using the authors' rubric): vs Retrieve-only it already gains +9.8pp on Tool (38.5 vs 28.7) and +9.7pp on Cultural (88.5 vs 78.8), while on General it exactly ties (71.3 vs 71.3). Everything beyond Action-only (Theory view + router + three fusion rules) adds +3.2/+1.1/+1.9pp — recomputed as 3, 3, and 1 task(s) at n=94/265/52, i.e., 7 tasks of 411 (+2.1pp mean). Theory-only never beats Retrieve-only in any domain. The ablation exists for only one of nine settings (BM25, Top3), and significance for these 1–3-task margins is deferred to Appendix B (unverifiable here); a per-setting ablation and a rubric-free LLM-judge baseline are what would be needed.
findings.why_it_matters: The paper's claimed contribution is the two-view + domain-routed framework, but the reported evidence attributes almost all of the +6.3pp headline gain to generic query-conditioned LLM scoring; the distinctively novel components are supported by single-digit task counts in a single retriever setting.
findings.verifier_note: Every number recomputes exactly. The Sec 5.3 baseline roster (ToolRerank 'algorithmic reranker', SkillFlow's ranking stage, mMARCO 'cross-encoder reranker', DEITA/M-DaQ/JQL 'assess intrinsic data quality') contains no rubric-free LLM prompted to rerank the shared candidate set, so the rubric's contribution is never isolated from generic LLM-judge capability. Action-only vs Retrieve-only (BM25): tie 71.3/71.3 General, +9.8 Tool, +9.7 Cultural — verified from Tables 3-4. M-SQE beyond Action-only: +3.2/+1.1/+1.9pp = 3/3/1 tasks at n=94/265/52 (integer-consistent: 70v67/94, 105v102/265, 47v46/52), 7 of 411 tasks, +2.1pp mean. Table 4's caption confirms the ablation covers only BM25/Top3 of nine settings. The obvious rebuttals — 'Action-only is our LLM-judge proxy' (it still uses the authors' rubric) and 'significance is in Appendix B' (unverifiable, and already conceded by the finding) — do not dissolve it. Theory-only indeed never beats Retrieve-only (67.0<71.3, 28.7=28.7, 59.6<78.8).

findings.title: Table 5's 'beneficial training-data constructor' conclusion rests on 3 net tasks out of 411, including a 0.0pp tie on Cultural
findings.location: Sec 5.5 'Downstream Trajectory Generalization' + Table 5 (p.7)
findings.evidence: Table 5: "Random 36.17 12.08 42.31 / Retrieve-only 36.17 12.83 50.00 / Base (untrained) 35.11 10.19 38.46 / M-SQE 38.30 13.21 50.00"; prose: "M-SQE yields the best fine-tuned model averagely in three domains... extending M-SQE from an inference-time filter to a beneficial training-data constructor."
findings.claim: Recomputed against task counts (n=94/265/52), the margins over Retrieve-only are +2.13pp General = 36/94 vs 34/94 (2 tasks), +0.38pp Tool = 35/265 vs 34/265 (1 task), and 0.00pp Cultural = 26/52 vs 26/52 (0 tasks). A one-task margin on 265 items cannot reach significance under any paired test, and Cultural — the domain where M-SQE's inference-time gain is largest (+11.6pp over Retrieve-only in Table 3, BM25) — shows exactly zero training-time benefit. The experiment's retriever and trajectory-construction configuration are also not stated in the provided text. The data supports at most 'no worse than Retrieve-only as a training-data selector', not the stated conclusion.
findings.why_it_matters: A named claim of the paper ('training-data constructor') is materially overstated relative to its own table; a rebuttal cannot dissolve this because the numbers are the paper's own and the significance ceiling is arithmetic.
findings.verifier_note: Table 5 arithmetic is integer-exact: General 36/94 (38.30) vs 34/94 (36.17) = net 2 tasks; Tool 35/265 (13.21) vs 34/265 (12.83) = net 1 task; Cultural 26/52 = 26/52 = net 0. Under McNemar/any paired test, net differences of 2, 1, and 0 can never reach significance (minimum two-sided p = 0.5 even with zero opposing discordants), so no appendix analysis could mathematically rescue the comparison. Cultural, where the BM25 inference-time gain is largest (90.4-78.8 = +11.6pp, verified), shows zero training-time benefit over Retrieve-only. Sec 5.5 and the Table 5 caption state no retriever, Top-N, or trajectory-construction protocol (the App F catch-all may cover it — unverifiable). The prose 'best fine-tuned model averagely' is numerically true (33.84 vs 33.00 avg, +0.84pp = 3 net tasks of 411), but 'extending M-SQE... to a beneficial training-data constructor' overclaims what 3 net tasks support. One nuance: if trajectories were built under Neural rather than BM25, the cultural contrast softens (Ne cultural inference gain is only +1.9pp) — but the finding already flags the config as unstated, and the core 2/1/0-task margins hold regardless.

findings.title: Every component of the evaluation universe is author-constructed; the 'mirrors today's ecosystem' claim is asserted, not validated
findings.location: Sec 5.2 (p.5), Sec 5.1 (p.4), Abstract (p.1), Table 1 (p.1)
findings.evidence: "The ecological-style layer approximates the naturally available material an agent would encounter today; it contains document-derived skills, rendered from existing community skill files, official product skills, and API documentation, and background-derived skills distilled from domain background documentation" (Sec 5.2); Abstract: "we build three-layer candidate skill pools mirroring today's ecosystem".
findings.claim: Every evaluated pool passes through author construction: the ecological layer is 'rendered'/'distilled' from real community and API material with a degree of transformation the provided text never specifies (deferred to Appendix E, unverifiable), and the MT/self-generated layers' defects come from the authors' chosen pipeline (varied only once, to Qwen3.6-Plus, in Fig 6 — a control on the synthesis LLM, not the curation process). Nothing in the provided material validates that the constructed defect distribution matches wild skill libraries, and no condition includes unmodified community entries — feasible at least for the ~79,700 audited English entries, even though the paper's own audit makes verbatim in-language pools impossible for Swahili/Hindi. Whether the ecological layer is near-verbatim is unverifiable pending Appendix E.
findings.why_it_matters: M-SQE's rubric detects the defects the authors chose to instantiate; if wild pools have a different defect distribution, the measured gains may not transfer, and the 'realistic multilingual pools' framing of the abstract is a construct-validity claim the design never tests.
findings.verifier_note: The underlying gap is real — no experiment validates the constructed defect distribution against wild skill libraries, and no condition uses unmodified community entries. But the claim as stated overreaches on three fronts a rebuttal would exploit. (1) 'Rendered from existing community skill files' is ambiguous between near-verbatim format conversion and substantive rewriting; the degree of transformation is deferred to Appendix E ('Detailed skill construction... are in Appendix E'), so 'rendered/distilled by the authors rather than sampled verbatim' asserts more than the provided text establishes. (2) 'No result... on a task set the authors did not construct' glosses over that Tool-Use uses 'real utterances from Kulkarni et al. (2025)' and Cultural/General tasks derive from six published external resources — author-filtered and rewritten, but externally sourced. (3) The proposed fix — a held-out subset 'sampled unmodified from the audited indexes' — is impossible in-language for the focus languages by the paper's own Table 1 (0 sw/hi entries); it is feasible only for the ~79,700 English entries. Fig 6's synthesis-LLM swap is correctly characterized as varying the synthesizer but not the rendering/curation process.

findings.title: The team that designed M-SQE's quality dimensions also rewrote and composed every evaluation task
findings.location: Sec 5.1 (p.4) and Sec 4.2 (p.3)
findings.evidence: "All task query rewriting and composition were carried out by the same multilingual expert team introduced in Section 4, through the same multiple rounds of review" (Sec 5.1); "A language-service expert team averaging over six years of professional experience constructs the dimensions across multiple rounds of review" (Sec 4.2).
findings.claim: The same expert team authored the rubric's agent-specific extensions, the task rewriting/composition, and (with the authors' pipeline) the defect-bearing pools, and the provided material contains no independently-authored task subset or third-party annotation of task failure modes to control the resulting construct-alignment risk — a risk distinct from text leakage, since Appendix E's control (unverifiable) governs string overlap, not taxonomy overlap. The risk is mitigated but not eliminated by the tasks' external benchmark origins and the rubric's grounding in a prior published taxonomy; an independently-composed task subset would resolve it.
findings.why_it_matters: Methods not built to the same taxonomy (the six baselines) are graded on a test whose difficulty axes were defined by M-SQE's designers; even absent bad faith, this systematically favors the proposed method.
findings.verifier_note: Both quotes are verbatim-accurate and the same-team authorship of rubric dimensions (Sec 4.2) and task rewriting/composition (Sec 5.1) is established, with no independent task subset or third-party failure-mode annotation in the provided text. But the finding overreaches in two ways. (1) Its two supporting examples (missing device-location slot; wrong red-envelope amount) are properties of POOL skills in Sec 4.4's running examples, not of task construction — so the direct evidence that tasks 'preferentially instantiate' rubric failure modes is thinner than claimed; the genuine alignment risk runs through the paired task-pool construction. (2) A rebuttal has real material: source tasks are 'drawn from real, published benchmarks' including 'real utterances from Kulkarni et al. (2025)', and the rubric dimensions are 'inspired by existing multilingual instruction-data quality taxonomy (Liu et al. 2026c)' — i.e., both endpoints of the alleged circle have external published anchors, and the team's rewriting is motivated by leakage control. The residual risk (same team extends the taxonomy, filters/rewrites tasks, and builds the defect-bearing pools; leakage control governs string overlap, not taxonomy overlap) is real but is a risk, not a demonstrated defect.

findings.title: Source-included pools guarantee a well-matched planted skill per query, so the motivating 'no usable in-language skill' regime is never evaluated
findings.location: Sec 5.2 (p.5); contrast Abstract and Sec 1 (p.1)
findings.evidence: "The pool is also source-included: a skill relevant to a given query may already sit inside it... Source inclusion is the standard convention in retrieval evaluation... Li et al. (2025) inject their own oracle skills into the retrieval index" (Sec 5.2); Abstract: "low-resource languages such as Swahili and Hindi have no in-language skill content"; Sec 1: "an agent serving these languages has no in-language skill to retrieve."
findings.claim: The protocol requires outputting Top-N always, so abstention or graceful degradation when no usable candidate exists is never measured, and the source-included design means the headline numbers largely measure ranking a relevant planted source above decoys (the text says a relevant skill 'may' sit in the pool; how often it is usable is unverifiable pending Appendix E). No condition isolates the introduction's motivating regime — a query facing a pool with no usable option, e.g., an English-only wild pool for a Swahili query — so the evaluation cannot show how M-SQE behaves precisely where the paper says the problem is worst. A defensible design for measuring selection, but the claims should be scoped to the synthesize-then-select regime.
findings.why_it_matters: The equality narrative rests on the zero-in-language-content scenario, yet the benchmark by construction never presents a query without a findable good skill; claims about that scenario are outside the evidence.
findings.verifier_note: Two elements are solid and verified: the selection protocol forces every selector to 'output a final selection of TopN skills' (Sec 5.3), so abstention/graceful degradation is structurally unmeasurable; and no reported condition isolates the zero-usable-option regime the introduction motivates with ('an agent serving these languages has no in-language skill to retrieve'). But the premise 'a usable source skill planted for every query by construction' overstates the text, which says only 'a skill relevant to a given query MAY already sit inside it' — and relevance is not usability. The paper's own numbers cut against the strong version: Tool-Use success tops out at 39.6-40.4% even for M-SQE (vs Prompt-only 20.4%), implying that for most tool queries no usable candidate is present or surfaced at K=20 — i.e., the benchmark does appear to contain a regime where the best available candidate fails, contradicting 'there is no condition where the pool's best candidate is genuinely defective'. The authors would also note their stated solution path is explicitly synthesize-then-select (Abstract, Sec 1), making the 'softened form' the intended object of study. The surviving defect is narrower than claimed.

findings.title: The domain taxonomy equals the benchmark's own partition; the 'five added examples' extensibility claim covers routing but not the hand-designed fusion adapter
findings.evidence: "the task domain τ is predicted from the query by a 5-shot prompted LLM domain router... reaching 98.5% accuracy on our three-domain query set"; "A new specialized domain can be added the same way: a new adapter paired with five added examples"; Fig 5 prose: "from +8.1pp at 10% corruption to +4.5pp at 90%".
findings.claim: The router's 98.5% accuracy is measured on the benchmark's own queries, where the three domains coincide with the three evaluation suites, so it measures suite-membership classification; deployment queries mixing domains are never tested. Extending to a new domain requires authoring a new expert-designed adapter — the genuinely expensive step, presented as lightweight ('a new adapter paired with five added examples') and never demonstrated — with the existing adapters' constants (0.6/0.4, Theory>=65, equal z-scores) justified by design rationale and perturbation deferred to Appendix C (unverifiable). The paper's own corruption sweep bounds correct routing's contribution at roughly 3.6-4.1pp of the +8.6pp BM25 margin, and the cultural rule — the only one folding Retrieval back in — operates in the domain where Retrieve-only is already strongest, consistent with (though not proof of) rules fitted to this benchmark's structure.
findings.why_it_matters: The router is presented as a framework pillar and an extensibility mechanism, but it is validated only against the benchmark's own partition, and the claim that new domains are cheap to add is unsupported by any experiment.
findings.verifier_note: Most components verify: 98.5% is measured 'on our three-domain query set' where domain labels coincide with suite membership; no mixed-domain or out-of-benchmark queries are tested; only C_cul folds Retrieval back in (C_gen=0.6A+0.4T, C_func=guard+Action), and Cultural is where Retrieve-only is strongest (78.8/88.5/90.4); the adapter constants are justified by 'design rationale' with perturbation in Appendix C (unverifiable); no fourth-domain addition is demonstrated; and the corruption-sweep bound recomputes (+8.1 at 10% vs +4.5 at 90% = ~3.6pp; ~4.1pp against the native +8.6pp BM25 margin from Table 3). But one clause is factually wrong and a rebuttal would seize it: 'The extensibility claim covers only the router's five examples' — the quoted sentence explicitly says 'a NEW ADAPTER paired with five added examples', so the paper acknowledges the adapter must be authored; the legitimate criticism is that adapter authoring is the expensive expert step presented as lightweight and never demonstrated. Additionally, the general class is defined as 'covering the rest' (a catch-all), so out-of-taxonomy queries have a designated route by design — the untested case is mixed-domain and distribution-shifted queries, not unroutable ones.

findings.title: Per-region and per-language equality claims rest on cells of roughly 8-16 tasks, where one task moves 6-12pp
findings.location: Fig 3 (p.6), Sec 2 (p.2), Table 2 (p.5), Abstract (p.1)
findings.evidence: Table 2: Cultural = 52 tasks over "Six main cultural regions"; General = 94 tasks over 6 languages; Sec 2: "strong gains in South Asia (+6.6pp) and Oceania (+8.4pp). This region-by-region consistency, not a single number, is the evidence that M-SQE's quality signal captures cultural correctness"; Abstract: "+12.9pp on Hindi and +5.6pp on Swahili".
findings.claim: 52 cultural tasks stratified over six regions leaves roughly 8-12 tasks per region, so each quoted regional delta (+6.6pp, +8.4pp) corresponds to about one task; General's ~16-task language cells include a 100.0 bar in Fig 3. The headline Hindi/Swahili gains are Tool-Use (~38 tasks/language if the 265 tasks split evenly), making +12.9pp about 5 tasks and +5.6pp about 2. Exact per-cell counts, per-cell uncertainty, and even Fig 3's retriever/backbone configuration are absent from the provided material (and the extracted bar labels cannot be unambiguously assigned to series). The paper explicitly offers region-by-region consistency as its evidence of cultural competence while operating at a granularity where single tasks produce the observed deltas.
findings.why_it_matters: The paper's distinctive selling point — language and cultural equality — is claimed at subgroup granularity the sample sizes cannot statistically support; per-cell Ns and intervals (or more tasks) are needed for these claims to stand.
findings.verifier_note: The arithmetic survives adversarial checking. 52 cultural tasks over six regions averages 8.7/cell (and +6.6pp is only integer-realizable at ~15 tasks, so cells are uneven or deltas are cross-config averages — either way each quoted delta is on the order of one task, as claimed with hedging). 94/6 = ~15.7 General tasks/language; 100.0 appears inside the extracted General-Languages block regardless of series attribution (which the finding correctly declines to assign). The headline +12.9pp Hindi / +5.6pp Swahili are explicitly Tool-Use (Sec 5.5) = ~5 and ~2 tasks at ~38/language under the flagged even-split assumption. Fig 3's caption and prose name no retriever or backbone (unlike Figs 4-6, which all say BM25), and no per-cell n or uncertainty appears in the provided material (Appendix B unverifiable). The strongest rebuttal — that 13/13 non-negative cells constitute joint sign-test-like evidence, per the paper's own 'region-by-region consistency, not a single number' framing — mitigates the consistency argument but cannot rescue the abstract's and contribution bullet's standalone per-language deltas (+12.9pp/+5.6pp), which are 2-5 task effects presented as headline results without reported uncertainty.

findings.title: The three 'quality scorer' baselines are query-agnostic by design and predictably lose, sometimes to Random or the no-skill floor
findings.location: Sec 5.3 (p.5), Table 3 (p.6)
findings.evidence: "six strong external baselines" (Sec 5.3); Table 3: DEITA Cultural (BM/Ne) 51.9/51.9 vs Random 60.0/65.4 and Retrieve-only 78.8/88.5; JQL Tool-Use (Ne) 20.4 = Prompt-only 20.4.
findings.claim: DEITA, M-DaQ, and JQL score intrinsic data quality with no query conditioning, so on a query-conditioned selection task they can rank a high-quality irrelevant skill over a relevant one; their losses (below Random in three cultural cells; one cell exactly at the no-skill anchor) are structural, not informative about M-SQE's merit. They function as an illustrative ablation of 'intrinsic quality alone is insufficient' — a point the paper itself argues in Sec 3 — rather than as competitors, and the "six strong external baselines" framing overstates them. Mitigating: the headline +3.5pp is computed against SkillFlow, the genuinely relevant skill-specific SOTA.
findings.why_it_matters: Padding the baseline table with guaranteed losers inflates the apparent breadth of superiority; only the reranker family constitutes a real comparison.
findings.verifier_note: All cited numbers verify: DEITA Cultural 51.9/51.9/75.0 sits below Random 60.0/65.4/79.2 in all three retriever cells (JQL likewise: 53.8/57.7/75.0), and JQL Tool-Use (Ne) 20.4 exactly equals the Prompt-only no-skill anchor 20.4. The paper's own Related Work concedes the structural point: quality scorers 'select instruction data on intrinsic quality alone' and the data-quality line 'stops at the data's own language quality' — so ranking them as three of 'six strong external baselines' on a query-conditioned selection task double-counts what Sec 3 already predicts will fail. The attempted rebuttal — that intrinsic-quality curation is a real deployed alternative — does not survive the setting: as post-retrieval selectors at fixed K they can rank a high-quality irrelevant skill over the relevant one by construction. The finding is appropriately scoped (minor), concedes the +3.5pp headline is against SkillFlow (verified: 69.1-65.6), and characterizes the trio correctly as an illustrative ablation of the paper's own motivating claim rather than competitors.

findings.title: 'Accepted paraphrase' checkers embed human acceptance sets whose authorship and freezing protocol are unstated in the main text
findings.evidence: "A response counts as correct only when it matches the checker's target exactly — a gold string or accepted paraphrase for General Skill Use and Cultural Skill Use"; "Checker acceptance criteria for each domain are detailed in Appendix G".
findings.claim: Determinism holds only at inference time; constructing the accepted-paraphrase sets is a judgment call, and the main text does not state who authored them, whether they were frozen before methods were compared, or whether their authors are independent of the team whose method is graded — load-bearing questions given that many General/Cultural margins are 1-4 tasks (e.g., Cultural 90.4 vs 88.5 is one task at n=52). This is unverifiable from the provided material rather than demonstrably wrong: Appendix G could resolve it with authorship, freezing, and inter-annotator evidence. The Tool-Use checker (exact function/slot match) does not share this concern.
findings.why_it_matters: At single-task margins, small differences in what counts as an acceptable paraphrase could flip cells; independence and pre-registration of acceptance sets is the standard safeguard and is not established in the main text.
findings.verifier_note: The quotes are verbatim (Sec 5.4) and the framing is already in the process-compliant 'unverifiable' form rather than 'missing'. Verified: determinism is an inference-time property; the construction of accepted-paraphrase sets is where judgment enters, and the main text states neither authorship, nor pre-freezing, nor independence from the evaluated method's team — while Sec 5.1's 'task query rewriting and composition were carried out by the same multilingual expert team' weakly suggests the same team built the targets, deepening rather than answering the question. The load-bearing stakes verify: Cultural 90.4 vs 88.5 is 47 vs 46 of 52 (one task), and several General/Cultural margins over the best baseline are 0-3 tasks (e.g., Cultural SF 94.2 vs 92.3 = 49 vs 48; Cultural Ne ties mMARCO at 90.4), with General Ne the outlier at 5 tasks. The concession that the Tool-Use exact function/slot checker is exempt is correct. Appendix G could resolve this with authorship, freezing, and inter-annotator evidence — which is exactly what the finding requests.

findings.title: No inference cost, latency, or call-count reporting for a method that adds up to ~100 LLM rubric calls per query over a zero-cost baseline
findings.location: Sec 5.3 (p.5), Sec 5.4 (p.6), Table 2 (p.5)
findings.evidence: "too deep inflates scoring cost and floods the candidate set" (Sec 5.3); Table 2 candidate depths K = 10/20/50; Sec 4.4: "we prompt a scorer LLM per view with its full rubric"; Sec 5.4 cites Gemini-3-Flash's "balance of multilingual quality and speed".
findings.claim: M-SQE issues two rubric calls per candidate (Theory is query-independent and thus cacheable per skill, though caching is never mentioned; Action is per query-skill pair), i.e., up to ~100 LLM calls per cultural query at K=50, versus zero marginal LLM cost for Retrieve-only and near-zero for the cross-encoder rerankers. No token, latency, or dollar figure appears anywhere in the provided material; the catch-all deferral ("all other implementation details are in Appendix F") may or may not cover it, but the main text carries none despite itself acknowledging scoring cost as a design constraint.
findings.why_it_matters: The practical question the paper's deployment framing raises — whether +6.3pp average is worth a 50-100x LLM-call overhead per query — cannot be answered from the paper.
findings.verifier_note: Verified by full-text scan: no token count, latency, or dollar figure appears anywhere in the provided nine pages. The call-count arithmetic holds: Sec 4.4 'we prompt a scorer LLM per view with its full rubric' = 2 calls per candidate; at Cultural K=50 (Table 2) that is up to ~100 LLM calls per query; the Theory view is 'independent of any particular query' and hence cacheable per skill, but caching is never mentioned. The baseline cost asymmetry is real (Retrieve-only: zero marginal LLM cost; mMARCO cross-encoder: K forward passes; ToolRerank: algorithmic). The paper itself treats scoring cost as a design constraint ('too deep inflates scoring cost', Sec 5.3) and picks Gemini-3-Flash for 'speed', yet reports no cost comparison in the main text. The finding correctly concedes the App F catch-all ('all other implementation details') may contain figures — making this an unverifiable-in-main-text gap, which is exactly how it is stated. Note Fig 4's '10 times the context' line concerns solver context, not scoring cost, so it does not answer the finding.

findings.title: The paper's core mechanism (prompted LLM rubric scoring of retrieved candidates + classic score fusion) is standard, and the literature establishing that is entirely uncited
findings.location: Sec 3 'Related Work' (p2, lines 178-182); Sec 4.4 (p3, lines 281-282); Sec 4 fusion rules (p4, lines 308, 324-325, 340-341); References (pp8-9)
findings.evidence: Sec 4.4: "we prompt a scorer LLM per view with its full rubric, obtaining the Theory and Action scores used throughout this section." Sec 3's entire reranker coverage: "Generic rerankers sharpen the retrieved list along the same axis: ToolRerank (Zheng et al. 2024) adapts hierarchy-aware reranking to tool retrieval, while mMARCO (Bonifacio et al. 2021) extends relevance reranking across languages." The reference list contains no LLM-as-reranker work (RankGPT/Sun et al., EMNLP 2023 Outstanding Paper, plus the 2023-2024 pointwise/pairwise/listwise prompting and RankVicuna/RankZephyr line - verified to exist and predate this work: https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.923/), no LLM-as-judge rubric-scoring work (MT-Bench judge, G-Eval, Prometheus, 2023-2024), and no post-retrieval document-critique RAG work (Self-RAG 2023, Corrective RAG 2024, which score retrieved documents' quality before use). The three fusion rules are likewise textbook: "Cgen = 0.6Action + 0.4Theory" (convex combination), "Cfunc ranks candidates by the lexicographic order (Theory >= 65, Action)" (threshold gate), and "Ccul = z(Retrieval) + z(Theory) + z(Action)" (z-normalized CombSum from the metasearch literature, Fox & Shaw 1994 / Montague & Aslam 2001, uncited).
findings.claim: Sec 3's related work omits the LLM-as-reranker literature (RankGPT and successors), the general LLM-as-judge rubric-scoring line (G-Eval, Prometheus), and the RAG document-critique line (Self-RAG/CRAG), and the three fusion rules use standard forms (convex combination, threshold gate, z-normalized CombSum) without citing score-fusion precedents — a citation-coverage gap the authors should close; however, the paper does engage its closest mechanism lineage by citing and empirically comparing LLM-based quality scorers (DEITA, M-DaQ, JQL) and by reimplementing SkillFlow, whose pipeline includes LLM-based post-retrieval selection, so this is a minor completeness issue, not an unsituated mechanism.
findings.why_it_matters: This inflates the apparent novelty of the framework layer: a reader of Sec 3 cannot tell that the contribution is the rubric content, the domain taxonomy, and the multilingual-skill setting rather than the scoring-then-fusing mechanism itself. It also has an experimental shadow: Table 3 contains no prompted-LLM reranker baseline (e.g., the same Gemini-3-Flash scorer given a generic RankGPT-style relevance/usefulness prompt), so the design never isolates 'same LLM, generic prompt' from 'same LLM, M-SQE rubric' - the comparison that would show the rubric, not the LLM, drives the gain. A rebuttal can add the citations, but the framing and the missing mechanism-matched baseline are the substantive issues.
findings.verifier_note: The bibliographic facts verify: the 36-entry reference list (pp8-9) contains no RankGPT-line LLM reranking, no G-Eval/Prometheus/MT-Bench LLM-as-judge work, no Self-RAG/CRAG document-critique work, and no metasearch fusion citation, and the fusion rules at lines 308, 324-326, 340-341 are indeed a convex combination, a threshold gate, and z-normalized CombSum. But the finding's framing fails on two points. (1) 'cites only pre-LLM rerankers' and 'never situates its mechanism against its closest lineage' is contradicted by the paper itself: the same Sec 3 paragraph (lines 176-178) covers SkillFlow's 'four-stage, skill-specific retrieval pipeline' whose fourth stage is LLM-based selection (per this reviewer's own external verification in the adjacent finding), and the paper cites, discusses (Sec 3 lines 192-197), and empirically compares three LLM-based quality scorers (DEITA, M-DaQ, JQL) as the 'Quality scorers' baseline family in Table 3 — the closest mechanism class (rubric/LLM scoring of candidate text) is engaged in both prose and experiments, with M-DaQ deployed in exactly the same post-retrieval selector role. (2) The paper claims no novelty for the fusion forms — line 355-359 presents the constants as design choices checked under perturbation (Appendix C) — so the uncited fusion classics are a courtesy citation, not a concealed-lineage problem. A rebuttal adding two sentences and three citations dissolves the 'major' severity; what survives is a real but ordinary related-work coverage gap that does not touch the qualified novelty claim (none of the missing works does multilingual skill quality estimation).

findings.title: The 'first' claim is narrow-but-true; all four qualifiers are load-bearing and the cited SOTA already contains a post-retrieval LLM selection stage for agent skills
findings.location: Sec 1 contribution bullet 1 (p2, lines 117-119); Sec 5.3 (p5, lines 475-478, 494-496)
