findings.evidence: "We propose M-SQE, to our knowledge the first post-retrieval quality estimation framework purpose-built for multilingual agent skills." The paper itself describes SkillFlow as "the state-of-the-art skill-specific retrieval pipeline (Li et al. 2025), faithfully reimplemented from its four-stage design" and reuses "SkillFlow (Li et al. 2025)'s own ranking stage ... as a post-retrieval selector." External verification (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06188): SkillFlow's four stages are dense retrieval, two cross-encoder reranks, and LLM-based selection - i.e., post-retrieval LLM selection over agent-skill candidates already exists in the cited SOTA, in English and relevance-oriented.
findings.claim: The 'first post-retrieval quality estimation framework purpose-built for multilingual agent skills' claim (lines 117-119) is accurate as worded, but its novelty rests entirely on the 'quality estimation (vs relevance)' and 'multilingual' qualifiers: post-retrieval LLM-based selection over agent-skill candidates already exists in the cited SkillFlow baseline that the paper reimplements, so the framework class is not new — reviewers should size the methodological contribution as those two qualifiers plus the constructed benchmark, which the paper itself declares.
findings.why_it_matters: The conjunction of four qualifiers is doing all the work in the headline novelty sentence. This is not a false claim, but reviewers and readers should weigh it as 'first to combine known pieces in a partly self-constructed setting' rather than 'first to conceive post-retrieval skill judgment' - the latter reading is invited by the surrounding prose but not supported.
findings.verifier_note: The quotes and the external SkillFlow verification hold, and the qualifier analysis is accurate: the 'first' claim (lines 117-119) is protected by 'quality estimation' and 'multilingual', and post-retrieval LLM selection over agent skills pre-exists in SkillFlow — which the paper openly acknowledges by reimplementing it (lines 475-478) and running its ranking stage as a baseline (lines 494-496), so nothing is hidden. But the finding's sharpest clause overreaches: 'the multilingual agent skills setting barely exists in the wild (Table 1: sw/hi at 0)' cherry-picks the two zero-count languages from a table that also shows roughly 5,000 genuine non-English in-language skill bodies (zh ~4,000, fr ~700, ko ~200, ja ~80, lines 51-54); the Tool Use tasks come from a published 52-language function-calling benchmark (Kulkarni et al. 2025, lines 393-396); and the self-constructed pools are declared, motivated as mirroring the practical MT+self-generation layering (Sec 5.2 lines 429-435), and released as a claimed contribution (lines 125-127). A rebuttal citing these facts defeats the insinuation that the setting is an artifact of the paper's own construction, leaving only the (accurate, self-conceded) observation about where the novelty load sits.

findings.title: Positioning overstates the data-quality line as judging 'only the data's own language quality', contradicting the paper's own description of DEITA two sentences earlier
findings.evidence: Line 196-197: "quality scorers such as DEITA (Liu et al. 2024) likewise select instruction data on intrinsic quality alone." Then line 197-199: "These pipelines judge only the data's own language quality, leaving out skill-use dimensions such as executability and context efficiency." And in the positioning paragraph: "The data-quality line, in turn, stops at the data's own language quality."
findings.claim: DEITA scores general instruction complexity and quality (an English-language, LLM-scored notion of intrinsic data quality), not 'language quality'; JQL scores multilingual pretraining-document quality in an education-value style. Reducing the whole line to 'language quality' is inaccurate for at least DEITA, and the paper's own earlier sentence ('intrinsic quality alone') is the correct characterization.
findings.why_it_matters: The operative contrast (static intrinsic quality vs execution-grounded, query-conditioned utility) is fair and survives; but the 'only language quality' wording paints the compared line as narrower than it is, which slightly pads M-SQE's claimed gap. A one-sentence rewording fixes it; as submitted it is an unfair characterization of a cited baseline family.
findings.verifier_note: I tried to refute this and could not. Quotes verified exactly: line 196-197 'quality scorers such as DEITA (Liu et al. 2024) likewise select instruction data on intrinsic quality alone' (accurate), then lines 197-199 'These pipelines judge only the data's own language quality' and lines 205-206 'The data-quality line, in turn, stops at the data's own language quality' (inaccurate for DEITA, which scores complexity and quality of English instruction/response data via LLM scoring — not linguistic/language quality in the sense this multilingual paper otherwise uses, i.e., translationese, mistranslation, localization, cf. lines 96-98 and dimensions 4-5 at lines 239-241). The charitable rebuttal ('language quality' = 'quality of the data as language material') concedes a rephrase to the paper's own correct wording one sentence earlier, which is precisely what the finding asserts. The finding is correctly self-limited: it does not claim the positioning gap (no executability/context-efficiency dimension in that line) is wrong — that gap holds for DEITA and JQL regardless — so it survives rebuttal as a precise minor wording defect.

findings.title: The verified-skill-synthesis line (SkillGen, CoEvoSkills) is cited but excluded from the positioning, and the citation bundle presenting them as multilingual synthesis misfits their scope
findings.location: Sec 1 (p2, lines 86-88); Sec 3 'Positioning M-SQE' (p3, lines 200-210); Sec 5.2 (p5, lines 450-453); References (SkillGen 'Verified Inference-Time Agent Skill Synthesis'; CoEvoSkills 'Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Co-Evolutionary Verification')
findings.evidence: Sec 1: "A practical way to close this gap is to synthesize more multilingual skills (Long et al. 2024; Ma et al. 2026; Wang et al. 2026)" - yet by their cited titles, Ma et al. 2026 (SkillGen: 'Verified Inference-Time Agent Skill Synthesis') and Wang et al. 2026 (SkillX: 'Automatically Constructing Skill Knowledge Bases for Agents') are general skill-synthesis works, and Long et al. 2024 is a synthetic-data survey; none is multilingual synthesis. Sec 3's positioning claims the skill-retrieval line "asks neither whether a matched skill is intrinsically sound, nor whether the skill will actually work for the task at hand" and names only two prior lines, while the paper's own description of Voyager in the same section says its "skill library lets an agent accumulate and reuse verified action sequences."
findings.claim: Sec 3's two-gap positioning (lines 200-206) omits a third line the paper itself cites — creation-time skill verification (Voyager's verified library, SkillGen, CoEvoSkills) — and never engages whether verified synthesis would shrink the Theory view's intrinsic-quality niche (the Action view's query-grounded role is safe by construction, and Sec 1 lines 88-98 already argues unverified MT/self-generation is unstable); additionally, the citations attached to 'synthesize more multilingual skills' (lines 86-88) are general synthesis works and a survey, none multilingual — a minor positioning and citation-precision gap.
findings.why_it_matters: Generate-and-verify is the most natural competing paradigm to retrieve-then-score: if pool skills arrived verified, much of the Theory view's job would be done upstream. The positioning would be strengthened, not weakened, by engaging this line explicitly; as written, the two-gap story is achieved partly by leaving the third line out, and the Sec 1 bundle mislabels two of these works as multilingual synthesis.
findings.verifier_note: Partly verified, partly wrong on location. Verified: Sec 3's positioning names exactly two lines ('The two lines above leave complementary gaps... M-SQE fills both', lines 200-206) and does not engage creation-time verification, despite the paper citing Voyager's 'verified action sequences' (lines 169-170), SkillGen ('Verified Inference-Time Agent Skill Synthesis', lines 852-855), and CoEvoSkills ('Co-Evolutionary Verification', lines 892-895); and the Sec 1 citation triple for 'synthesize more multilingual skills' (lines 86-88) is, by the cited works' own titles, general synthesis work plus a synthetic-data survey, none multilingual. But the claim 'the paper never argues why creation-time verification does not shrink the niche... its implicit answer is in Sec 5.2, not in the positioning' misreads the paper: the argument appears in the introduction immediately after the synthesis citation — lines 88-98 argue that MT and self-generation 'neither is stable in quality', citing Li et al. 2026 (self-generated skills can hurt) and Liu et al. 2026c (MT content errors) — and the positioning paragraph itself claims the Action view measures 'how much a specific skill will help the query at hand' (lines 208-210), which no creation-time verifier can supply. So the niche defense exists for realistic unverified pools and for the Action view; what the paper genuinely never addresses is the narrower Theory-view overlap: whether verified synthesis (SkillGen-style), if adopted, would obviate selection-time intrinsic-quality certification.

findings.title: Citation practice: two references never cited in the main text, thin support for a 'widely adopted' claim, and several load-bearing roles filled from one overlapping-author cluster
findings.location: References p8 (Hu et al. 2022 LoRA, lines 769-772; Karpukhin et al. 2020 DPR, lines 779-783); Sec 5.4 (p6, lines 576-579); Secs 4.2, 5.3 (taxonomy and baselines)
findings.evidence: Grep of the full provided text: Karpukhin et al. 2020 and Hu et al. 2022 appear only in the reference list, never in the body (presumably used in supplementary Appendix F, which I cannot see). Sec 5.4: Gemini-3-Flash is "chosen for its balance of multilingual quality and speed, a trade-off widely adopted in recent multilingual agent research (Liu et al. 2026a,b)" - the sole support for 'widely adopted' is two papers (MADE, GaoYao) whose author lists heavily overlap with each other and with MIDB (Liu et al. 2026c) and M-DaQ (Zhao et al. 2026). Counting the 36 references: roughly 15-16 receive substantive individual treatment (a specific claim, role, or reimplementation attached); the rest are bundled cites, dataset/repo pointers (LittleDinoC, wshobson, huzey; six culture datasets), or unanchored; 9 of 36 are 2026 arXiv preprints (normal for this field, noted, not itself a defect).
findings.claim: One overlapping-author research cluster (MIDB, M-DaQ, MADE, GaoYao, CultureScope, SAGE — 6 of 36 refs) supplies the Theory-view taxonomy's cited inspiration, one of the three quality-scorer baselines, two of the six culture task sources, and the only citations behind the 'trade-off widely adopted in recent multilingual agent research' claim (line 579), which should either cite independent work or be softened — though the backbone choice itself is separately supported by the Fig. 6 robustness sweep; separately, Hu et al. 2022 and Karpukhin et al. 2020 are uncited in the provided main text and their usage (presumably Appendix F) is unverifiable from the provided material.
findings.why_it_matters: None of this is misconduct and the key external premises verified accurate (see strengths). But 'widely adopted' resting on a two-paper same-cluster bundle is weak support for a design decision, and the concentration of taxonomy, baseline, and backbone justification in one line means the paper's framing of the multilingual-quality literature is narrower than the field; the orphan references should be anchored or moved to the supplementary bibliography.
findings.verifier_note: I re-ran the grep myself: 'Hu et al.'/'LoRA' and 'Karpukhin'/'Dense Passage' appear only in the reference list (lines 769-772, 779-783), never in the provided body — the orphan observation is factually correct. findings.title: The Theory cap rule's dimension classes are undefined, and under the only available reading the two agent-specific dimensions are uncapped
findings.location: Sec 4.2, p.3 (paper_clean.txt lines 235, 248-257) vs Sec 4.4, p.4 (line 332)
findings.evidence: Sec 4.2 defines the taxonomy: "(1) Correctness (red-line)" and "organizing them into two blocks: general quality dimensions — correctness, completeness, cross-lingual faithfulness, and localization — and agent-specific dimensions — executability and context efficiency". The cap rule then reads: "The overall Theory score is the six-dimension mean on a 0–100 scale, capped at 40 if the red-line dimension is violated and at 80 if any basic dimension is, so a single severe defect cannot be averaged away." Grep confirms "basic" occurs exactly once in the paper (line 256) — it is never defined, and neither named block is called "basic". Sec 4.4 then invokes "candidates whose Theory scoring flags a language red-line", but the cap rule says "the red-line dimension" (singular) and only Correctness carries the red-line marker; the language dimensions (cross-lingual faithfulness, localization) sit in the general-quality block. Recomputation: if "basic" = the general-quality block (the only parseable reading), a skill scored 0 on Executability and 100 elsewhere gets mean 500/6 = 83.3 with NO cap applying — a single severe agent-specific defect IS averaged away, contradicting the rule's stated purpose, and doing so precisely on the dimensions the positioning claims prior data-quality work lacks ("leaving out skill-use dimensions such as executability and context efficiency", lines 198-199). (The binary predicate "violated" on 0–100 dimension scores is also never given in the main text; the rubric is in unprovided Appendix D, so that prong is unverifiable rather than missing.)
findings.claim: The Theory cap rule's operative classes are undefined in the main text: 'basic dimension' (line 256) occurs once, is never defined, and matches neither named block ('general quality' vs 'agent-specific', lines 248-252), and Sec 4.4's 'language red-line' (line 332) has no referent in a taxonomy that marks only Correctness '(red-line)' and speaks of 'the red-line dimension' in the singular (lines 235, 255). Whether the two agent-specific dimensions — the paper's claimed differentiators over prior data-quality work (lines 198-199) — carry any cap is therefore indeterminate: under the reading basic = non-red-line they are capped at 80, but under the block-based reading they carry no cap at all, and an otherwise-perfect skill with Executability = 0 scores 500/6 = 83.3 with the 'single severe defect cannot be averaged away' guarantee silently failing on exactly those dimensions. (The binary 'violated' predicate on 0-100 scores is deferred to unprovided Appendix D, hence unverifiable rather than missing.)
findings.why_it_matters: No known finding touches the Theory cap rule, the red-line/basic terminology, or the Sec 4.2/4.4 taxonomy mismatch; prior passes covered the fusion constants' justification, not the cap system's internal coherence.
findings.verifier_note: Verified facts: 'basic' occurs exactly once (line 256) and is never defined; the two named blocks are 'general quality dimensions' and 'agent-specific dimensions' (lines 248-252), neither called 'basic'; only Correctness carries the '(red-line)' marker (line 235) and the cap rule says 'the red-line dimension' singular (line 255), while Sec 4.4 invokes an undefined 'language red-line' (line 332); 500/6 = 83.3 recomputes. New: no known finding touches the cap rule or the 4.2/4.4 taxonomy. But the claim's linchpin — 'the only available reading of basic' is the general-quality block — fails: the cap sentence's own red-line-vs-basic contrast supports the equally (arguably more) natural reading basic = any non-red-line dimension, under which all five non-Correctness dimensions including the agent-specific pair carry the 80 cap and the anti-averaging rule is coherent. So 'internally inconsistent' and 'the guarantee fails for a third of the dimensions' are not established as arithmetic fact, only as one branch of an ambiguity; the language-red-line contradiction prong is real but is also the shared substance of the confirmed guard finding. Real defect, overstated conclusion; severity sits at the minor/major boundary and is best merged with tool-use-guard-inconsistent-with-cap-arithmetic.

findings.title: The Tool-Use guard's stated semantics are arithmetically inconsistent with the Theory caps for the paper's own two examples
findings.location: Sec 4.4 "Tool-use quality guarding", p.4 (lines 324-339), against the cap rule in Sec 4.2, p.3 (lines 254-257)
findings.evidence: "The threshold of 65 marks the boundary below which a skill is structurally unusable on the 0–100 Theory scale — for example, missing a required slot or carrying a critical localization failure — and candidates whose Theory scoring flags a language red-line are guarded out the same way." Under Sec 4.2, localization is a general-quality (non-red-line) dimension and slot coverage falls under Completeness/Executability, also non-red-line; a violated non-red-line dimension caps Theory at 80, not 40. Recomputation: an otherwise-excellent skill with Localization = 0 scores min(500/6, 80) = min(83.3, 80) = 80 ≥ 65, so it PASSES the guard Cfunc = M·1[Theory ≥ 65] + Action; for the six-dimension mean itself to fall below 65 the dimension sum must be < 390, i.e. with one dimension at 0 the other five must average below 78 — the skill must already be broadly mediocre. Only a Correctness (red-line) violation, cap 40 < 65, is guaranteed to fail the guard. The escape clause — treating localization failures as a "language red-line" capping at 40 — contradicts Sec 4.2's singular "the red-line dimension" = Correctness; alternatively, if "flags" denotes a mechanism separate from the score, that flag appears nowhere in the Cfunc formula, whose only inputs are Theory and Action.
findings.claim: The 65 threshold cannot deliver the gating behavior the paper uses to justify it: by the paper's own cap arithmetic, both illustrative "structurally unusable" defects (missing required slot, critical localization failure) can score Theory = 80 and pass the guard, so either the guard's stated semantics are false or the cap taxonomy of Sec 4.2 is — one of the two subsections must be wrong, and Tool-Use is the domain carrying the headline Hindi/Swahili gains.
findings.why_it_matters: Prior passes questioned whether the 0.6/0.4 and 65 constants were justified and ablated; no known finding checks whether the caps and the guard threshold are mutually coherent as arithmetic, which they are not.
findings.verifier_note: Every element re-verified. Quotes check out (lines 324-339): the guard is Cfunc = M·1[Theory >= 65] + Action, and the paper claims 65 'marks the boundary below which a skill is structurally unusable — for example, missing a required slot or carrying a critical localization failure', then claims concretely that 'The guard removes such a candidate from contention first' for the slot-omitting smart-home skill, echoing Fig. 1's 'Theory view screens out this gap'. Recomputed: Localization = 0 with five 100s gives min(500/6, 80) = 80 >= 65 under every reading of 'basic' (Localization is non-red-line on any reading), so the paper's own example defect passes the guard; a missing required slot maps to Completeness/Executability by the paper's own definitions (Fig. 1 says 'omits'), cap 80 or none, same result; mean < 65 requires sum < 390, i.e. the other five dimensions averaging below 78 — broad mediocrity, not the single structural defect the text describes; only the Correctness 40-cap guarantees failure. Rebuttals all die: reading localization failures as a 40-capped 'language red-line' contradicts the singular '(red-line)' = Correctness of Sec 4.2; a score-independent flag has no channel into Cfunc, whose only inputs are Theory and Action; 'the rubric scores such skills lower in practice' concedes the stated cap arithmetic does not deliver the stated gating and defers to unprovided Appendix D. New: no known finding examines cap/threshold coherence (the known list has nothing on the caps or the 65 threshold at all). Major is warranted — Tool-Use carries the headline Hindi/Swahili gains and Fig. 1 is the flagship mechanism narrative.

findings.title: The scalar Action score used by all three fusion rules is never defined, and the inverse orientation of Misleading risk blocks any default reading
findings.location: Sec 4.3, p.3 (lines 262-279) and Sec 4.4, p.4 (lines 308, 326-327, 340-341); Action-only row of Table 4, p.6
findings.evidence: Sec 4.3 gives "five grounded-fit dimensions plus an explicit risk estimate", "(6) Misleading risk: the chance that a related-looking skill steers the solver to a wrong API, value, or convention", "Each dimension is scored 0–100", and only a qualitative closure: "the rubric permits a high Action score only when the procedure is executable, the constraints match, and the misleading risk is low". Unlike the Theory view ("The overall Theory score is the six-dimension mean ... capped ..."), no aggregation of the six Action dimensions into the single "Action" appearing in Cgen = 0.6Action + 0.4Theory, Cfunc = M·1[Theory ≥ 65] + Action, and Ccul = ... + z(Action) is ever stated. A Theory-style six-dimension mean is not a coherent default because dimension (6) is inversely oriented — a naive mean would reward high misleading risk; whether risk is reversed, subtracted, thresholded, or kept separate is unstated. Consequently "any M larger than the Action range" (line 326-327) invokes a range that is itself formally unfixed (e.g. [0,100] for a mean of five vs [-100,100] if risk is subtracted). The prose compounds the ambiguity: "The single mixing coefficient gives task applicability a modest majority" (lines 314-316) treats the 0.6 weight as if it applied to dimension (1) alone. Appendix D holds "the full scoring rubric", so the aggregation is unverifiable from provided material — but the main text is asymmetric on its own terms, defining Theory's aggregation while leaving Action's, used in every formula and the Table 4 Action-only ablation, undefined.
findings.claim: A load-bearing quantity of the framework — the Action scalar consumed by all three domain rules and one ablation row — has no stated definition in the main text, and the risk dimension's orientation means no default aggregation can be inferred, leaving Eq. 1's components and Cfunc's offset constant M formally underdetermined.
findings.why_it_matters: The known deferred-details finding lists prompts, decoding, checkers, task lists, the dense retriever, and the fine-tuning recipe — not the score definition; the known strength "scoring math fully specified at formula level" covers the three fusion formulas, whose shared input is exactly what is never defined.
findings.verifier_note: Re-verified against lines 262-284, 308, 314-316, 324-327, 340-341, and Table 4 (line 610). The main text defines Theory's aggregation explicitly ('six-dimension mean ... capped') but for Action gives only 'Each dimension is scored 0-100' plus the qualitative 'the rubric permits a high Action score only when ... the misleading risk is low'; no rule turning six dimension scores into the single Action scalar is ever stated. The orientation point is decisive against any inferred default: dimension (6) is 'the chance that a related-looking skill steers the solver to a wrong API' — higher = worse — so a naive mean is incoherent, and reversal/subtraction/thresholding/holistic-LLM-assignment are all live, mutually inconsistent possibilities. Consequences recomputed and real: Action is the shared input of Cgen, Cfunc, and Ccul; 'any M larger than the Action range' (lines 326-327) invokes a range that varies by resolution (e.g. [0,100] vs [-100,100]); Table 4's Action-only row is not re-runnable from the main text; and the prose 'gives task applicability a modest majority' (lines 314-315) conflates dimension (1) with the whole view. Newness holds: known finding #44's deferred-items list (prompts, decoding, checkers, task lists, dense retriever, fine-tuning recipe) does not include the score definition, and the known strength 'scoring math fully specified at formula level' covers the three fusion formulas, not their undefined shared input — this finding is the precise correction to that strength. The candidate already calibrates the Appendix D deferral correctly (unverifiable, not missing) while resting on the genuine main-text asymmetry, so the rebuttal 'it is in the rubric appendix' does not remove the finding. Tried and failed to kill it.

findings.title: Ccul z-scores a per-candidate "Retrieval" quantity the formalism never defines, and z(·) is undefined for zero-variance candidate sets
findings.location: Sec 4.4 "Cultural evidence fusion", p.4 (lines 340-342), against Sec 4.1, p.3 (lines 222-224) and Sec 5.3, p.5 (lines 470-478)
findings.evidence: "Ccul = z(Retrieval) + z(Theory) + z(Action), where z(·) denotes per-query z-score standardization within the retriever's candidate set." But Sec 4.1 types the retriever as returning only a set — "the retriever returns a candidate set CK = R(q, S, K)" — with no per-candidate score, and no raw Retrieval scalar is defined anywhere else (its only other appearances, lines 231, 295, 352, are qualitative). The three retrievers have heterogeneous native outputs — BM25 lexical scores, a hybrid dense retriever, and "SkillFlow, the state-of-the-art skill-specific retrieval pipeline ... faithfully reimplemented from its four-stage design" — and whether a four-stage pipeline exposes a final scalar at all, or only a rank, is unstated. Separately, z-score standardization divides by the within-candidate-set standard deviation, which is zero whenever a view assigns all K candidates equal scores — a case the Theory caps make non-hypothetical (scores clustering at the 80 cap) — leaving Ccul undefined (0/0) with no stated fallback.
findings.claim: The cultural fusion rule Ccul = z(Retrieval) + z(Theory) + z(Action) consumes a 'Retrieval' scalar the paper never defines: the problem formulation returns only a candidate set (CK = R(q, S, K), no per-candidate score), the term's other three appearances are qualitative, and for one of the three evaluated retrievers — SkillFlow, 'faithfully reimplemented from its four-stage design' — it is not even clear a final scalar exists rather than a rank; additionally, the per-query z-standardization has no stated fallback for the zero-variance case where a view scores all K candidates identically. Both are presumably resolved in unprovided Appendix F, so this is a main-text specification gap (the formula is not instantiable from the provided material for at least one retriever), not a demonstrated error — minor.
findings.why_it_matters: Known findings cover the candidate-depth formula's degeneracy and the deferral of the concrete retriever model, not the formal undefinedness of the Retrieval score or the z-score's degenerate cases.
findings.verifier_note: Core verified: Ccul = z(Retrieval) + z(Theory) + z(Action) (lines 340-342); the formulation types the retriever's output as a bare set CK = R(q, S, K) (lines 223-224); grep confirms 'Retrieval' as a quantity appears only at lines 230, 295, 340, 352, never as a defined scalar; the three retrievers are heterogeneous, and whether the 'faithfully reimplemented ... four-stage' SkillFlow pipeline exposes a final scalar rather than a rank is genuinely unstated; z-standardization's zero-variance case has no stated fallback. New: known #17 is the K-formula's sub-1,000-pool degeneracy and #44 defers the concrete dense retriever — neither touches the Retrieval scalar or z edge cases. But two overstatements force WEAKENED: (1) 'the cultural domain's entire fusion rule is not well-defined' — BM25 and the hybrid dense retriever have obvious native scores, so the sharp gap is confined to the SkillFlow instantiation plus the formalism-level omission, and 'all other implementation details are in Appendix F' (line 569) makes this an unverifiable-from-provided-material specification gap, not a demonstrated defect; (2) the zero-variance case being 'non-hypothetical' via Theory scores clustering at the 80 cap requires all K = 50 candidates to tie on a view, which is speculation, and any implementation's standard z = 0 fallback fully answers it. Survives only in the narrowed form, at minor severity.

findings.title: Fig. 3's absolute levels run against the supply narrative built on it: Chinese (~4,000 skills) is worst in both language panels, zero-supply Hindi is Tool-Use's best, and "can actually rely on" rests on 41-55% success

findings.evidence: General bars (fr,hi,ja,ko,sw,zh): "66.7 68.3 87.7 100.0 89.6 56.9"; Tool-Use bars (en,fr,hi,ja,ko,sw,zh): "45.8 36.6 54.6 37.4 28.3 41.1 27.2"; Table 1: zh ~4,000, en ~79,700, sw/hi 0; Social Impact: "A skill pool that was only usable by chance becomes one an agent serving an underserved-language community can actually rely on."

findings.title: The core cross-lingual-harm premise is an asserted analogy, and the abstract credits its borrowed effects to 'our audit'
