findings.evidence: Abstract: "our audit finds that low-resource languages such as Swahili and Hindi have no in-language skill content, so retrieval often returns a skill written in a different language than the query, degrading accuracy and recall." Sec 1: "Lu et al. (2026) show that when a query and its supporting evidence are written in different languages, both answer accuracy and evidence recall drop sharply, possibly due to the distribution mismatch introduced by cross-lingual retrieval. Skills play exactly this evidentiary role for an agent. An agent that retrieves an English skill for a Swahili or Hindi query therefore inherits the same mismatch failure mode". Sec 2 hardens it to categorical fact: agents are "in practice, less capable on their behalf."
findings.claim: The paper's central harm premise is an untested analogical transfer: Lu et al. (2026)'s cross-lingual evidence-retrieval finding (deep-research QA) is carried to agent skills by the bare assertion 'Skills play exactly this evidentiary role,' the hedged mechanism ('possibly due to the distribution mismatch') becomes deductive ('therefore inherits the same mismatch failure mode'), and Sec 2 hardens it to categorical fact ('in practice, less capable on their behalf'). No experiment in the paper tests the premise — no in-language vs cross-language skill-provision comparison exists in Tables 3-5 or Figs 3-6, though the built pools would have made one straightforward. The abstract further asserts the borrowed effects in the paper's own voice as the consequence chained to its audit ('so retrieval often returns a skill written in a different language than the query, degrading accuracy and recall'): the degradation is never measured in the paper, and 'recall' is not a metric anywhere in its evaluation — its only other occurrences are the Lu et al. paraphrase (line 75) and the unrelated depth-rule rationale (line 482); all reported results are task-success rates.
findings.why_it_matters: Known findings verify the other two motivational premises (70.1% adoption; curated-vs-self-generated) and critique the evaluated regime (source-included pools), but none addresses the Lu et al. transfer, the untested mismatch premise, or the abstract's attribution of borrowed effects to the audit.
findings.verifier_note: Core verifies: quotes are verbatim (lines 11-14, 73-80, 133-135); grep confirms 'recall' occurs exactly 3 times (abstract line 14, Lu et al. paraphrase line 75, depth-rule line 482) and is never a reported metric — every result table/figure reports task-success rates; no experiment conditions on the language of the provided skill (checked Tables 3-5, Figs 3-6, including Fig 6's pool-synthesis variation, which varies the synthesis LLM, not skill language). Novelty holds: known items verify the other two motivational premises (70.1% adoption; curated-vs-self-generated) and the pool-regime elision, but none touches the Lu et al. transfer or the abstract's borrowed-effect assertion. One prong dies under rebuttal: with audited in-language supply exactly 0 for Swahili/Hindi, retrieval from the audited ecosystem is necessarily cross-language for those languages, so the audit does license 'often' (it is if anything conservative) — the 'frequency never measured' sub-claim cannot be sustained as an error. The untested-transfer, hedge-to-deduction, and foreign-metric ('recall') prongs survive.

findings.title: The stated leakage rule ('share no content-bearing terms with the answer key') is untenable for Tool-Use's exact function/slot answer keys and is contradicted by the paper's own worked examples
findings.location: Sec 5.1 (p.4, lines 373-380) vs Sec 5.4 (p.6, lines 561-567) and Sec 4.4 examples (p.4, lines 316-318 and 333-336)
findings.evidence: Sec 5.1: "All three domains are built by one construction process... (3) leakage control, rewriting task prompts into natural user queries that copy no text from any pool skill and share no content-bearing terms with the answer key (Appendix E)." Sec 5.4: correctness for Tool Use is "an exact function/slot execution match... the correct function name with matching argument slots" (no accepted-paraphrase provision, unlike General/Cultural). Sec 4.4's own examples: "Consider a smart-home skill retrieved for 'turn off the bathroom light'" (device-location slot = bathroom) and "when a query asks for an XLOOKUP formula" (gold answer is that formula).
findings.claim: Read literally against the Tool-Use checker definition ('the correct function name with matching argument slots,' with no accepted-paraphrase provision unlike General/Cultural), the universal leakage rule — natural queries 'share no content-bearing terms with the answer key' — cannot hold for tool-use tasks whose gold calls contain query-supplied slot values with language-invariant surface forms (media titles, proper names in the 'media playback' and 'calendars and alarms' categories), nor generally for the English-language subset, where common-noun slot values (device, location) must appear in any natural query. 'Content-bearing terms' must therefore carry an unstated narrower construal (e.g., excluding user-supplied slot values and protecting only the answer's distinctive content such as the function name); the term is never defined in the main text, and the operative leakage protocol for the domain carrying 265 of 411 tasks and the +12.9/+5.6 headline deltas is in unavailable Appendix E — so the stated rule is imprecise as written and its actual construal is unverifiable from provided material. Severity: minor.
findings.why_it_matters: Known findings cover paraphrase-checker authorship, construction circularity, and deferred run details, but none examines the internal coherence of the three-stage filter's leakage rule against the Tool-Use checker definition or the paper's own examples.
findings.verifier_note: Quotes verify verbatim (lines 378-380, 561-567, 316-317, 333-334) and 20.4 = 54/265 recomputes. But the incompatibility thesis is overstated on three fronts. (1) For 6 of 7 tool-use languages, translation naturally breaks surface-term overlap with an English canonical call (sw 'bafuni' vs slot value 'bathroom') while fully preserving slot determinability — the rule and checker are jointly satisfiable there, so 'cannot both be literally true' fails as a universal. (2) The Prompt-only 20.4% prong is invalid: the leakage rule constrains query wording, not the solver's ability to map paraphrases/translations to canonical values semantically, so solvers producing exact calls without lexical overlap demonstrates no incoherence. (3) The Sec 4.4 'bathroom light'/'XLOOKUP' passages are schematic mechanism illustrations, not documented benchmark queries, and for the answer's core content (function name, gold formula) the rule is coherent and well-motivated: the query describes intent, the skill supplies the canonical answer. What survives: for query-supplied slot values with language-invariant surface forms (media titles, proper names — 'media playback' and 'calendars and alarms' are named task categories) and for the English-language subset (en is in the roster), literal compliance with 'share no content-bearing terms with the answer key' is impossible unless 'content-bearing' carries an unstated narrower construal; the term is undefined in the main text and the operative protocol is in unavailable Appendix E. That residue is a precision/verifiability gap (minor), not the claimed incompatibility (major), and it is distinct from the known blanket deferral finding because of the internal-tension element.

findings.title: Sec 5.2 claims every candidate is 'judged on its own content alone', but the paper's only defined anonymization is applied at solver hand-off, not at scoring
findings.location: Sec 5.2 (p.5, lines 462-464) vs Sec 4.1 (p.3, lines 226-229)
findings.evidence: Sec 5.2: "The pool is also source-included: a skill relevant to a given query may already sit inside it, but every candidate is judged on its own content alone." Sec 4.1 defines stripping only for the solver: "the downstream solver receives only the query and the anonymized skill bodies in Z_N (provenance labels and source identifiers stripped), without any gold answer or checker metadata."
findings.claim: Blinding is operationalized only at the solver hand-off: Sec 4.1 strips 'provenance labels and source identifiers' from Z_N (implying such metadata exists in the pipeline), but no statement operationalizes anonymization of the candidate set C_K that M-SQE's scorer LLM and all selector baselines judge. Sec 5.2's defense of source inclusion — 'every candidate is judged on its own content alone' — asserts the property at the selection stage without any stated mechanism, and the scorer prompts that would verify it are in unprovided Appendix F, so the guarantee is unverifiable from provided material. This matters because scoring is exactly where visibility of layer provenance (ecological vs MT vs self-generated) or source identifiers would give a quality-correlated shortcut directly favoring planted source skills.
findings.why_it_matters: Known items record solver-side blinding as a stated strength and critique source-included pools for eliding the motivating regime; none notices that the content-only-judging claim at the scoring stage is asserted without any specified blinding mechanism.
findings.verifier_note: Factual core verifies by exhaustive grep: the only anonymization/stripping language in the paper is at lines 226-228 ('the anonymized skill bodies in Z_N (provenance labels and source identifiers stripped)'), which is the solver hand-off; the parenthetical confirms provenance metadata exists in the pipeline; no statement operationalizes anonymization of C_K for the scorer LLM (Sec 4.4: 'we prompt a scorer LLM per view with its full rubric') or the selector baselines. Novelty holds: known items record solver-side blinding as a strength and critique source inclusion, but none notes the scoring-stage asymmetry. One clause overreaches, though: 'nothing in the main text rules it out' is not quite right — Sec 5.2's 'every candidate is judged on its own content alone' (line 463) is itself a declarative protocol claim that, taken at face value, rules out provenance visibility at scoring. The accurate form of the finding is asserted-but-not-operationalized: the mechanism backing the claim is stated only for the solver, and the scorer prompts that would settle it are deferred to unprovided Appendix F ('all other implementation details'), making the guarantee unverifiable from provided material rather than absent.

findings.title: 'Faithfully reimplemented' SkillFlow — the SOTA retriever and the headline +3.5pp comparator — carries no reported reproduction check
findings.evidence: "SkillFlow, the state-of-the-art skill-specific retrieval pipeline (Li et al. 2025), faithfully reimplemented from its four-stage design"; its ranking stage is also "reused here as a post-retrieval selector regardless of which retriever supplied its candidates"; the headline is "+3.5pp over the strongest baseline, SkillFlow (65.6%)".
findings.claim: Fidelity is asserted by adverb only: the reimplementation is 'from its four-stage design' (i.e., from the paper description), and no calibration against Li et al.'s published results on their own benchmark is reported or even referenced anywhere in the provided material (Appendix F promises 'implementation details', not a validation). Because this single author-built reimplementation serves as both the strongest retriever and the strongest baseline defining the abstract's +3.5 margin, an under-tuned reimplementation would silently inflate the headline, and the claim of faithfulness is unverifiable from provided material.
findings.why_it_matters: Known findings cover the margin's thinness and deferred run details, and a known strength credits adversarial reuse of the closest competitor; none addresses the absence of any fidelity validation for the reimplemented comparator itself.
findings.verifier_note: I tried to kill this and failed. Quotes verify verbatim (lines 475-477, 494-496, 584-585). Exhaustive grep for faithful/calibrat/reimplement/replicat/reproduce finds only 'faithfully reimplemented' — no fidelity evidence is claimed, reported, or referenced anywhere in the provided material, and no appendix is invoked for validation (App F is cited only for 'implementation details'), so nothing here is even a deferred claim. Recomputed: SkillFlow row avg = 590.5/9 = 65.6 (strongest baseline; next is mMARCO 63.0), M-SQE = 622.1/9 = 69.1, margin exactly +3.5pp; SkillFlow is also the strongest retriever under both selection anchors (Retrieve-only SF column 74.5/37.4/90.4 and Random SF column 70.6/33.1/79.2 are column maxima in every domain), so the same author-built reimplementation defines both the candidate pools' best retriever and the headline comparator. Rebuttals fail: code release enables future checking but reports none; 'original benchmark differs' does not excuse the standard fidelity check of reproducing the original paper's numbers with the reimplementation. Novelty holds: known items cover margin thinness (1-5 task margins, significance in unprovided App B) and credit adversarial reuse of the closest competitor as a strength, but none addresses reimplementation fidelity.

findings.title: Sec 2's 'only usable by chance becomes one ... can actually rely on' is contradicted by the paper's own absolute numbers (Swahili 41.1% post-M-SQE)
findings.location: Sec 2 (p.2, lines 149-151) vs Fig 3 Tool-Use panel (p.6, lines 513-523) and Table 3 anchors (p.6, lines 542-544)
findings.evidence: Sec 2: "A skill pool that was only usable by chance becomes one an agent serving an underserved-language community can actually rely on." Fig 3 (M-SQE, pooled over three retrievers): Hindi 54.6, Swahili 41.1. Table 3 Tool-Use anchors: Prompt-only 20.4 (=54/265); Random 26.1/26.6/33.1 (mean 28.6).
findings.claim: Sec 2's claim that the pool 'becomes one an agent serving an underserved-language community can actually rely on' is not supported by the paper's own absolute levels: after M-SQE, Swahili tool-use succeeds on 41.1% of tasks (majority failure) and Hindi on 54.6% (Fig. 3, M-SQE pooled over three retrievers). The sentence's other half ('only usable by chance') should not be attacked: domain-level Tool-Use Retrieve-only (28.7/25.7/37.4, mean 30.6) sits within 2.0pp of Random (26.1/26.6/33.1, mean 28.6) and below it under the Neural retriever, and no per-language Random anchor is reported, so pre-M-SQE relevance-only selection being roughly chance-level is consistent with the paper's numbers.
findings.why_it_matters: Known Sec 2 findings address the deltas' comparator, their 1-2-task granularity, and the unmeasured equality construct; none addresses this sentence's absolute-level claims (chance-before, reliable-after) against the paper's own success rates and anchors.
findings.verifier_note: Prong 1 verifies: the sentence (lines 149-151) sits in the tool-use paragraph of Sec 2, and Fig 3's tool-use panel (M-SQE pooled over three retrievers, per the verified facts) shows Swahili 41.1% (majority failure) and Hindi 54.6% — absolute levels that do not support 'can actually rely on'; no known item addresses this sentence (known Sec 2 items cover the deltas' comparator/granularity and the unmeasured equality construct). Prong 2 fails under rebuttal: (a) the implied pre-levels (54.6-12.9=41.7; 41.1-5.6=35.5, arithmetic checked) are per-language, while the Random anchor is language-pooled (mean (26.1+26.6+33.1)/3 = 28.6), and no per-language Random exists — Hindi, the strongest tool-use language, could plausibly have a per-language chance level near 41.7, so 'demonstrably usable far beyond chance' is not demonstrable; (b) worse for the candidate, at domain level pre-M-SQE relevance selection really was approximately chance: Tool-Use Retrieve-only (28.7/25.7/37.4, mean 30.6) sits +2.0pp from Random (26.1/26.6/33.1, mean 28.6) and below it under Neural (25.7 vs 26.6), which is the natural quantitative reading of 'only usable by chance'; (c) 'usable by chance' does not deny above-no-skill-floor utility, so 'roughly double the 20.4% floor' (1.7x for Swahili, in fact) does not contradict it.

findings.title: The abstract, overview, Fig 2, contribution bullet, and conclusion all describe a two-view score, but the cultural rule gives the retriever's raw relevance an equal one-third weight
findings.location: Sec 4.4 (p.4, lines 340-341) vs Abstract (lines 18-21), Sec 1 contribution framing (lines 107-110), Sec 4 overview (lines 214-217), Fig 2 caption (lines 187-189), Conclusion (lines 735-737)
findings.evidence: Sec 4.4: "C_cul = z(Retrieval) + z(Theory) + z(Action), where z(.) denotes per-query z-score standardization within the retriever's candidate set." Elsewhere the method is uniformly two-view: "scores candidates via a Theory view ... and an Action view ..., unified into a domain-conditioned final score" (abstract); "M-SQE then scores every candidate from two complementary views ... The two views are routed into a single score" (overview); "judges a retrieved skill on its own merits and on its fit to the query, then routes the two judgments by the task's domain" (conclusion).
findings.claim: For the cultural domain — where M-SQE posts its highest absolute results (90.4/90.4/94.2) and Sec 2 stakes its cultural-equality claim — one-third of the 'post-retrieval quality estimation' score is the retriever's own relevance score re-entering with equal standardized weight, disclosed only inside Sec 4.4 ('and, for cultural tasks, Retrieval'). Every framing statement (abstract, contribution, overview, Fig 2 caption, conclusion) describes exactly two judgments, misdescribing the mechanism in the domain where retrieval strength (Retrieve-only 78.8-90.4) already carries most of the performance; the conclusion's 'routes the two judgments' is flatly inaccurate for one of the three domains.
findings.why_it_matters: Known findings cover the ablation's Action-only dominance, Fig 3 aggregation, and fusion-line citation gaps, but none records that the paper's own self-description as a two-view quality estimator contradicts the cultural rule's equal-weight Retrieval term.
findings.verifier_note: I tried to kill this and failed. Grep confirms the Retrieval term appears exactly twice, both inside Sec 4.4 (the parenthetical at lines 294-295 and the formula C_cul = z(Retrieval)+z(Theory)+z(Action) at lines 340-341, with per-query z-standardization giving the three terms equal weight); every other self-description is two-view — abstract (lines 18-21), Sec 1 ('two complementary views', line 108; 'how the two views combine', line 114), Sec 2 ('two-view quality estimation', line 136), Fig 2 caption ('scored by Theory and Action views', line 188), Sec 4 overview ('The two views are routed into a single score', line 216), results discussion (lines 652, 669, 720), and the conclusion ('routes the two judgments by the task's domain', line 736). Numbers verify: cultural M-SQE 90.4/90.4/94.2 is the paper's best absolute domain, Sec 2 stakes its cultural-equality claim there, and Retrieve-only already reaches 78.8/88.5/90.4 (87-96% of M-SQE's level), so the omitted term re-injects the signal that already carries most cultural performance. The 'abstracts may compress' rebuttal fails because the Sec 1, Sec 4 overview, and conclusion sentences are affirmative mechanism descriptions contradicted by the three-term rule for one of three domains. Novelty holds against the ablation, Fig-3-aggregation, fusion-citation, and scoring-math-strength items. Only tone needs a trim: 'flatly inaccurate' becomes 'inaccurate for the cultural domain'.

findings.title: Fig 6's own data: upgrading the pool synthesizer lowers every method's success and halves M-SQE's margin, contradicting the quality-bottleneck premise and the 'ruling out pool-synthesis artifacts' claim
findings.location: Fig. 6 and 'LLM Backbone Robustness', Sec. 5.5, p. 7 (paper_clean.txt lines 670-722)
findings.evidence: Fig 6, scorer held at Gemini-3-Flash: with Qwen3.5-9B synthesis, Retrieve-only/M-SQE = 59.6/68.2 (Gemini solver) and 57.0/66.0 (Qwen solver); after 'rebuilding the MT and self-generated pool layers with a stronger Qwen3.6-Plus', the same cells read 57.9/61.4 and 53.6/58.5. Recomputed: the stronger synthesizer LOWERS Retrieve-only by 1.7/3.4pp and M-SQE by 6.8/7.5pp, cutting M-SQE's margin from +8.6/+9.0 to +3.5/+4.9 — roughly halved. The text says only that this 'retains positive gains for both solvers' and concludes the controls are 'ruling out pool-synthesis artifacts and scorer or solver bias as explanations for the gains.'
findings.claim: Fig. 6's synthesis-upgrade control (scorer fixed at Gemini-3-Flash) moves in a direction the paper never explains: rebuilding the MT and self-generated layers with the 'stronger' Qwen3.6-Plus LOWERS every printed cell — Retrieve-only by 1.7/3.4pp and M-SQE by 6.8/7.5pp across the two solvers — and roughly halves M-SQE's margin (+8.6/+9.0 -> +3.5/+4.9). A drop in the scorer-free Retrieve-only baseline, and a ~7pp drop in M-SQE's absolute success on a higher-quality pool, are not predicted by the paper's quality-bottleneck premise and go undiscussed (the text says only that the change 'retains positive gains for both solvers'). Because the synthesis choice modulates the gain magnitude by roughly 2x, the concluding sentence 'ruling out pool-synthesis artifacts ... as explanations for the gains' overstates what the control shows — gains persist, but their headline size is not robust to pool synthesis — and the main results are reported at the weak-synthesizer operating point (justified only as 'representative'), which is also the gain-maximizing setting among those tested.
findings.why_it_matters: Both known Fig 6 findings concern only delta-label arithmetic vs endpoints; no known finding examines the direction or magnitude of the synthesis-upgrade effect or its tension with the paper's premise and its 'ruling out' sentence.
findings.verifier_note: Arithmetic fully verified against Fig 6 (paper_clean.txt lines 679-703): with scorer fixed at Gemini-3-Flash, the Qwen3.6-Plus rebuild lowers Retrieve-only 59.6->57.9 / 57.0->53.6 and M-SQE 68.2->61.4 / 66.0->58.5, cutting margins +8.6/+9.0 -> +3.5/+4.9; row 1 is provably the main setting (matches Table 3 macro averages exactly), and its margins are the maximum of all six cells. Novel: known Fig 6 items cover only delta-label/endpoint mismatches. But 'contradicts the premise' overshoots: a SHRINKING margin under better synthesis is what the quality-bottleneck premise predicts. The genuine, unexplained anomalies are the absolute drops (including the scorer-free Retrieve-only baseline, and M-SQE falling ~7pp on a supposedly higher-quality pool), which the text papers over with 'retains positive gains for both solvers'. The 'rewards planted-skill matching' horn is speculation, and the weak-synthesizer operating point is explicitly justified as 'representative' (Sec 5.4), blunting the cherry-picked-operating-point reading. The 'ruling out' critique survives as an overstatement claim: with the gain magnitude modulated ~2x by synthesis choice, pool synthesis remains a partial explanation of the headline margins.

findings.title: Two Fig 6 cells that must be identical by construction differ (Retrieve-only 59.6 vs 59.5 under a scorer swap), giving the only direct evidence of run-to-run noise — on the order of the paper's 1-2-task headline margins
findings.location: Fig. 6, p. 7 (paper_clean.txt lines 679-695) vs Sec. 5.3 definition of Retrieve-only (line 489)
findings.evidence: Retrieve-only is defined as 'the retriever's own ranking' — it uses no scorer LLM. Fig 6 rows 1-2 hold pools (Qwen3.5-9B) and solver fixed and vary ONLY the scorer (Gemini-3-Flash vs Qwen3.6-Plus), so their Retrieve-only cells must be identical. Under the Qwen solver they are (57.0 = 57.0), but under the Gemini solver they differ: 59.6 vs 59.5. The 59.6 equals the Table 3-derived macro average exactly ((71.3+28.7+78.8)/3 = 59.6); the 59.5 deviates. Recomputed: one Tool-Use task flip moves the three-domain macro average by 0.126pp — matching the 0.1pp gap.
findings.claim: A structurally scorer-independent quantity takes two different values across scorer rows, so either the supposedly deterministic pipeline exhibits ~1-task test-retest nondeterminism (undisclosed, and of the same size as 5 of the 9 per-cell wins the known findings show are 1-5 task margins) or a figure cell was transcribed/edited inconsistently — and neither possibility is acknowledged anywhere.
findings.why_it_matters: Prior passes checked each Fig 6 delta against its own endpoints and each table cell against task-count grids, but never checked cross-row invariants (which cells are forced equal by the method's definition); this also strengthens [random-row-aggregation-and-run-variance-unstated] and [per-cell-margins-below-significance-threshold] with the paper's only measured noise datum.
findings.verifier_note: Verified and failed to kill. Retrieve-only is 'the retriever's own ranking' (line 489) — no scorer, no router. Fig 6 rows 1-2 share pools (Qwen3.5-9B synthesis), retriever (BM25), and solver column, varying only the scorer, yet the Gemini-solver Retrieve-only cells read 59.6 vs 59.5 (the Qwen-solver cells are identical at 57.0). Recomputed: 59.6 equals the Table 3 BM25 macro average exactly (unrounded 59.6007 — no rounding path of the same underlying counts can yield 59.5), while exactly one Tool-Use task flip (100/265/3 = 0.126pp) gives 59.475 -> 59.5. So the disjunction is exhaustive: undisclosed run-to-run nondeterminism (~1 task, the same order as 5 of the 9 per-cell wins the known findings show are 1-5 task margins) or an inconsistently transcribed results cell; neither is acknowledged. Novelty checked: [fig6-delta-labels-inconsistent]/[fig6-deltas-contradict-printed-endpoints] concern delta labels vs their own endpoints (7.0 vs 7.1, 5.0 vs 4.9) — a within-cell check; no known finding tests cross-row invariants forced by the method's definitions, and no known finding involves the 59.6/59.5 pair. One phrasing nit folded into the corrected claim: the paper claims deterministic CHECKERS/objective, not deterministic solver decoding (decoding is deferred), so 'supposedly deterministic pipeline' is glossed precisely.

findings.title: The paper's flagship novelty, the Theory view, standalone performs below Random on Cultural and below Retrieve-only on General — replicating the exact failure mode the paper attributes to its query-agnostic quality-scorer strawmen
findings.location: Table 4 and 'Ablation Study', Sec. 5.5, p. 6 (paper_clean.txt lines 600-613) vs Table 3 BM25 columns (lines 542-544)
findings.evidence: Table 4 (BM25, Top3): Theory-only = 67.0 / 28.7 / 59.6. Table 3, same BM25/Top3 setting: Random = 66.2 / 26.1 / 60.0; Retrieve-only = 71.3 / 28.7 / 78.8. So Theory-only loses to uniform-Random on Cultural (59.6 < 60.0; 31/52 vs 60.0%), loses to Retrieve-only on General (67.0 vs 71.3, -4.3pp) and Cultural (-19.2pp), and only exactly ties it on Tool-Use (28.7 = 28.7 = 76/265). The ablation prose states only 'M-SQE beats both single views on all three domains' and never discloses the sub-anchor placement. Theory-only's Cultural 59.6 sits inside the quality-scorer baseline band (DEITA 51.9, M-DaQ 63.5, JQL 53.8) that the paper frames as structurally inadequate.
findings.claim: Sec. 3 presents 'the Theory view brings intrinsic quality estimation to skill-use time' as one of M-SQE's two gap-filling contributions, but the paper's own ablation shows intrinsic quality estimation adds no standalone selection value: Table 4's Theory-only (67.0/28.7/59.6; BM25, Top3) trails Retrieve-only by 4.3pp on General and 19.2pp on Cultural, exactly ties it on Tool-Use (76/265), and on Cultural is statistically indistinguishable from the Random anchor (59.6 vs 60.0) while landing inside the band of the query-agnostic quality-scorer baselines (DEITA 51.9 - M-DaQ 63.5) that the paper frames as structurally inadequate. The ablation prose compares single views only against full M-SQE, one table below the anchors, and never discloses this at-or-below-anchor placement — leaving the Theory view's demonstrated value confined to its small guard increment over Action-only (the known 7-of-411-task margin).
findings.why_it_matters: [missing-plain-llm-judge-baseline] notes Action-only captures nearly all the gain and [quality-scorer-baselines-structural-mismatch] notes the external query-agnostic scorers predictably lose, but no known finding states that the paper's OWN Theory view lands below the Random/Retrieve-only anchors, i.e., that it behaves like the strawmen it is contrasted against.
findings.verifier_note: Numbers verified: Theory-only 67.0/28.7/59.6 = 63/94, 76/265, 31/52; vs Table 3 BM25 Retrieve-only 71.3/28.7/78.8 it trails by 4.3pp (4 tasks) on General and 19.2pp (10 tasks) on Cultural and exactly ties on Tool-Use (76/265 both); on Cultural it sits 0.4pp below Random (60.0) and inside the DEITA/M-DaQ/JQL band (51.9-63.5). The ablation prose indeed compares single views only to full M-SQE. Novel: no known finding records that the paper's OWN intrinsic-quality view lands at-or-below the do-nothing anchors, mirroring the query-agnostic baselines it dismisses. Weakened on three points: (a) the 0.4pp Cultural deficit to Random is under one task (1 task = 1.92pp) against a multi-draw average — 'statistically indistinguishable from Random' is the defensible phrasing, not 'worse than random selection'; (b) 'entire demonstrated value is the +7-task guard effect' restates the known [missing-plain-llm-judge-baseline] quantity (recomputed 3+3+1=7 tasks) — only the sub-anchor placement is new; (c) 'conceals' imputes intent, and an author can note components were never claimed to work standalone and that the prose flags 'visibly uneven' gaps and frames Theory as a guard — the surviving criticism is nondisclosure of the anchor comparison and its bearing on the Sec. 3 gap-filling positioning.

findings.title: Per-language results invert the supply gradient the equality narrative rests on (zero-supply Hindi is best, 4,000-skill Chinese is worst), and provably unequal per-language task sets make all cross-language comparisons task-mix-confounded
findings.location: Fig. 3 Tool-Use panel, p. 6 (paper_clean.txt lines 513-524) vs Table 1 (lines 49-59) and Sec. 5.5 (lines 592-599)
findings.evidence: Sec. 5.5 reads Fig 3 through the audit: 'These are the two languages whose in-language skill supply Table 1 measures at zero, so the improvement of M-SQE relieves exactly where the ecosystem leaves speakers with the least.' But the Fig 3 Tool-Use M-SQE ordering is hi 54.6 > en 45.8 > sw 41.1 > ja 37.4 > fr 36.6 > ko 28.3 > zh 27.2, while Table 1 supply is en 79,700 > zh 4,000 > fr 700 > ko 200 > ja 80 > sw 0 = hi 0: the zero-supply language is BEST, the second-best-supplied (zh) is WORST (also lowest in the General panel, 56.9), and English (79,700 skills) trails Hindi by 8.8pp. Moreover 265/7, 94/6, and 52/6 are all non-integer, so per-language/per-region task sets are provably unequal in size and hence not parallel — even though the Tool-Use source is described as a single '52-language function-calling benchmark' from which parallel per-language sets could have been drawn.
findings.claim: Fig. 3's cross-language claims rest on non-parallel task sets: tasks are 'stratified across languages' (each task in one language), 265/7, 94/6, and 52/6 are all non-integer, and no single per-language task count below 72 makes the printed en (45.8) and hi (54.6) Tool-Use rates simultaneously achievable — so the per-language subsets provably differ in size and content, and every cross-language comparison of levels or deltas (the abstract's 'lifts the lowest-resource languages most', Fig. 3's 'largest gains on Hindi and Swahili') conflates task-mix composition with language identity. Consistent with this, benchmark levels anti-track the audited ecosystem supply the social-impact narrative invokes: zero-supply Hindi is the best Tool-Use language (54.6, +8.8pp above English with ~79,700 skills) while second-best-supplied Chinese is worst in both Tool-Use (27.2) and General (56.9). Within-language deltas remain valid, but the Sec. 5.5 inference that the improvement 'relieves exactly where the ecosystem leaves speakers with the least' — and any between-language reading — is uncontrolled for what tasks each language happens to contain.
findings.why_it_matters: [subgroup-equality-claims-underpowered] and [region-claims-single-task-resolution] concern cell SIZE and [headline-deltas-comparator-and-scope] the missing comparator; no known finding addresses non-parallel task composition across languages or the supply-success inversion that undercuts the 'relieves exactly where supply is least' reading.
findings.verifier_note: Facts verified: Fig 3 Tool-Use M-SQE ordering hi 54.6 > en 45.8 > sw 41.1 > ja 37.4 > fr 36.6 > ko 28.3 > zh 27.2 against Table 1 supply en 79,700 > zh 4,000 > fr 700 > ko 200 > ja 80 > sw=hi=0; zh is also lowest in General (56.9); hi-en = +8.8pp. Non-parallelism strengthened by recomputation: beyond 265/7, 94/6, 52/6 being non-integer, no common per-language task count below 72 tasks (pooled N<216 over 3 retrievers) makes en=45.8 and hi=54.6 jointly achievable, so en and hi provably have different task counts under any remotely parallel design. Novel: known items ([subgroup-equality-claims-underpowered], [region-claims-single-task-resolution], [headline-deltas-comparator-and-scope]) attack cell size and comparator ambiguity, not subset non-comparability or the supply-success inversion. Weakened: (a) 'shows the per-language numbers track authorial task/pool composition choices' overclaims — the inversion shows levels do NOT track ecosystem supply, but language-intrinsic effects are an unexcluded alternative to composition; (b) the quoted Sec 5.5 sentence is a DELTA claim, which the LEVEL inversion does not directly contradict — it undermines the benchmark-to-ecosystem bridge; (c) the assertion that parallel sets 'could have been drawn' from the 52-language source relies on background knowledge of MASSIVE-Agents' parallel design, not the provided text; (d) within-language deltas remain internally valid — the confound attaches only to between-language readings.

findings.title: Task selection from source benchmarks is unauditable: the 52-to-7 language restriction of Kulkarni et al. is never justified, and no domain reports how many candidate tasks entered vs. survived the three-stage filter
findings.location: Sec. 5.1, pp. 4-5 (paper_clean.txt lines 361-395, 416-427)
findings.evidence: 'Tool Use draws on real utterances from Kulkarni et al. (2025)'s 52-language function-calling benchmark, restricted to seven languages (en, fr, hi, ja, ko, sw, zh)' — no criterion for the restriction is given anywhere (the roster silently coincides with Table 1's seven audited languages, an implicit rationale at best). The filter is described ('verifiability... skill necessity, screening out tasks that saturate without any skill... leakage control') and 'Each domain then stratifies the admitted tasks across its languages, regions, and originating benchmarks', but no attrition counts, stratification quotas, or per-source composition appear for any domain — e.g., the 52 Cultural tasks come from six named resources (NormAd, CultureBank, CulturALL, CultureScope, CultureAtlas, SAGE) with no per-source breakdown, ~8.7 tasks per resource. Appendix pointers cover leakage (E), checkers (G), and a catch-all 'all other implementation details' (F), none promising selection/attrition statistics.
findings.claim: The task-selection policy is unauditable from the provided material: the Tool-Use source is restricted from 52 languages to seven with no stated criterion (the roster silently equals Table 1's audit set, itself unjustified); the three-stage filter (verifiability / skill-necessity / leakage) reports no entered-vs-admitted attrition counts for any domain; and no per-source or per-language stratification counts are given (e.g., the 52 Cultural tasks across six named resources, ~8.7 per resource). None of the named appendix pointers (E: leakage, G: checkers, F: catch-all) promises selection or attrition statistics. Since the headline claims are per-language deltas on exactly these author-selected subsets, favorable selection cannot be excluded from the provided material — an auditability gap additional to, though partially overlapping, the known circularity and author-constructed-universe findings.
findings.why_it_matters: [core-run-details-deferred] concerns re-runnability (task lists deferred) and [rubric-task-team-circularity] concerns who rewrote tasks; no known finding addresses the selection POLICY — the unjustified 52-to-7 restriction and the absent entered-vs-survived accounting that would rule out cherry-picking.
findings.verifier_note: Textual facts verified: 'restricted to seven languages (en, fr, hi, ja, ko, sw, zh)' (lines 392-394) with no stated criterion anywhere (the roster silently equals Table 1's audit set, itself never justified); the three-stage filter reports no entered-vs-admitted counts for any domain; no per-source or per-language stratification counts (52 Cultural tasks over six resources, ~8.7 each); appendix pointers E/G/F promise leakage, checkers, and a catch-all, not selection statistics — and the candidate correctly frames the conclusion as 'cannot be ruled out from the provided material' since catch-all Appendix F could in principle contain attrition data. Novelty holds for the atoms: no known finding mentions the 52-to-7 restriction or filter attrition ([core-run-details-deferred] is re-runnability, [rubric-task-team-circularity] is authorship). Weakened because: (a) the cherry-picking implication substantially overlaps the substance of [rubric-task-team-circularity] and [no-external-evaluation-universe], which already establish author control of the evaluation universe; (b) the language-restriction leg is blunted by the obvious implicit rationale an author rebuttal will supply (the audited supply-spectrum roster of Table 1) — the candidate itself concedes this; (c) 'equality claim scoped to 13%' applies only to the Tool-Use domain's source benchmark, not the paper's equality claims generally. As corrected, this is an auditability-specifics addition to an established concern, closer to minor than major.

findings.title: Sec. 5.1's provenance promise ('Source tasks are drawn from real, published benchmarks') is never fulfilled for the General domain, which names only a construction 'paradigm', not a source
findings.location: Sec. 5.1, p. 4 (paper_clean.txt lines 368-369 and 386-391)
findings.evidence: The construction preamble states: 'Source tasks are drawn from real, published benchmarks and culture resources (detailed below).' The detail delivers a named source for Tool Use (Kulkarni et al. 2025) and six named resources for Cultural, but for General only: 'General Skill Use covers 94 curated multilingual skill-use tasks across six languages (fr, hi, ja, ko, sw, zh), built in the SkillsBench paradigm (Li et al. 2026)' — a paradigm is a method, not a source, and SkillsBench is cited elsewhere only for its 'checker-verified construction'. Whether the 94 multilingual tasks were translated from any published benchmark or authored outright by the expert team is never stated.
findings.claim: Sec. 5.1 promises 'Source tasks are drawn from real, published benchmarks and culture resources (detailed below)', and the detail delivers named sources for Tool Use (Kulkarni et al. 2025) and Cultural (six resources) but none for General: its 94 tasks (23% of the evaluation, and the domain containing General-Ne, the second-largest per-cell margin at 5 tasks) are described only as 'curated' and 'built in the SkillsBench paradigm (Li et al. 2026)' — a construction method, not a source. Whether these multilingual tasks were adapted from any published benchmark or authored outright by the expert team is never stated, so the paper's own sourcing claim goes unfulfilled for one of three domains — closing off the natural 'our tasks come from real benchmarks' rebuttal to the known author-constructed-universe concern.
findings.why_it_matters: [no-external-evaluation-universe] asserts the universe is author-constructed and the ecosystem-mirror claim unvalidated, but no known finding identifies the specific textual contradiction that the 'drawn from real, published benchmarks' sentence goes unfulfilled for the General domain.
findings.verifier_note: Core verified: the preamble 'Source tasks are drawn from real, published benchmarks and culture resources (detailed below)' (lines 368-369) is fulfilled by name for Tool Use (Kulkarni et al. 2025) and Cultural (six resources) but not for General, which gets only 'curated ... built in the SkillsBench paradigm (Li et al. 2026)' — a construction method (the same paragraph cites SkillsBench for its 'checker-verified construction'); whether the 94 tasks derive from any published benchmark or were authored outright is never stated; 94/411 = 22.9%. Novel: [no-external-evaluation-universe] asserts author construction generally; no known finding pins the unfulfilled '(detailed below)' sourcing promise to the General domain, and the candidate is right that this pre-empts the natural rebuttal to that known finding. Two overstatements force WEAKENED: (a) the evidence detail 'the domain contributing M-SQE's largest per-setting margin count in General-Ne' is FALSE — recomputed per-setting margins over the strongest baseline make Tool-Use/BM25 the largest (+6.4pp, 17 tasks), with General-Ne second by pp (+5.3pp, 5 tasks); (b) 'internal contradiction' overshoots — an author could rebut that the tasks were adapted from SkillsBench material, so the demonstrable defect is an unfulfilled/ambiguous sourcing claim, not a proven contradiction.

findings.title: The Cultural domain's query language(s) are never specified — Table 2's language column lists regions instead — and the MT layer's 'language roster' for that domain is therefore undefined
findings.location: Table 2, p. 5 (paper_clean.txt lines 397-408) and Sec. 5.2 (lines 445-449); Sec. 5.1 Cultural paragraph (lines 416-427)
findings.evidence: Table 2's column 'Query language/culture' reads 'fr, hi, ja, ko, sw, zh' for General and 'en, fr, hi, ja, ko, sw, zh' for Tool Use, but for Cultural Skill Use only 'Six main cultural regions' — no language is ever named for the 52 cultural queries, and the six cited source resources are English-language benchmarks. Sec. 5.2 states 'MT skills are translated from each domain's English source material into its non-English target languages, so a domain's MT volume follows its language roster' — yet the Cultural domain's 1,283 MT skills follow a roster that appears nowhere in the paper.
findings.claim: The Cultural domain — carrier of the cultural-equality headline — never states what language its queries are in: Table 2's 'Query language/culture' column lists languages for General and Tool Use but only 'Six main cultural regions' for Cultural, and no cultural query language appears anywhere in the main text. The gap propagates to the pool: Sec. 5.2 defines each domain's MT layer as translated 'from each domain's English source material into its non-English target languages' following 'its language roster', yet the roster behind Cultural's 1,283 MT skills is never given, and the Action view's 'Language fit' dimension (usability 'in the query's language') is uninterpretable for this domain. If the 52 queries are English (their MT source material is stated to be English, and the cited resources are English-dominant, though CulturALL is explicitly multilingual), the domain exercises the multilingual machinery only on the candidate side and its results do not speak to serving non-English speakers — and the main text does not permit deciding which reading holds.
findings.why_it_matters: Known cultural findings target gold-answer essentialism, region taxonomy, and cell sizes; none notices that the Cultural row breaks Table 2's own language column or that the domain's MT 'language roster' is undefined.
findings.verifier_note: Core verified and genuinely new: Table 2's 'Query language/culture' column lists languages for General (fr,hi,ja,ko,sw,zh) and Tool Use (en+6) but only 'Six main cultural regions' for Cultural (line 404); no language for the 52 cultural queries appears anywhere in the main text (Sec 5.1 Cultural paragraph, Sec 2, and Fig 3 all speak only of regions); Sec 5.2 defines each domain's MT layer by 'its language roster' and 'its non-English target languages' (lines 447-449), yet the roster behind Cultural's 1,283 MT skills is never given; and the Action view's 'Language fit: the prose is usable in the query's language' dimension is uninterpretable for this domain. No known cultural finding (essentialism, region taxonomy, cell sizes) or reporting finding touches this. Weakened on one evidence point: 'the six cited source resources are English-language benchmarks' is asserted as fact, but CulturALL's own reference entry reads 'Benchmarking Multilingual and Multicultural Competence' — explicitly multilingual — and the other resources' languages are not stated in the provided material; the supportable anchor is Sec 5.2's statement that MT translates 'from each domain's English source material'. The equality-impact leg therefore must remain conditional, as the candidate's own phrasing partly acknowledged.

strengths.title: Table 3 is arithmetically airtight, down to implied integer task counts
strengths.why: All ten row averages recompute exactly from the nine cells (e.g., M-SQE 622.1/9=69.12->69.1; SkillFlow 590.5/9=65.61->65.6; M-DaQ's printed 53.5 matches the average of implied unrounded counts, 53.55, showing averages were computed from unrounded values). Every deterministic row is consistent with integer correct-counts over the stated task totals 94/265/52 (e.g., M-SQE = 70/94, 75/94, 72/94, 105/265, 96/265, 107/265, 47/52, 47/52, 49/52); the only row failing the integer test is Random — exactly the one anchor expected to be seed-averaged. This is the signature of real, carefully tabulated results.

strengths.title: The 9-setting dominance claim verifies, even under a stricter reading than the paper states
strengths.why: "First or tied-first against the single strongest baseline in all 9 domain-by-retriever settings" holds vs SkillFlow (margins +3.2/+5.3/+2.1/+6.4/0.0/+3.0/+3.9/+3.9/+3.8), and also holds against the best baseline per column (ties only at Tool-Neural 36.2 vs SkillFlow and Cultural-Neural 90.4 vs mMARCO). "+3.5pp over the strongest baseline, SkillFlow (65.6%)", "+6.3pp over Retrieve-only" (recomputed 6.29; per-setting margins +1.9 to +11.6, all positive), "+14.0pp over Random" (13.98), and "strictly ahead of both selection anchors in all 9 settings" all recompute exactly. Notably, Sec 5.5 states each comparator explicitly — the comparator hygiene problems are confined to the abstract and Sec 2.

strengths.title: Fig 3 reconciles exactly with Table 3 under forensic recomputation — the figures plot real data
strengths.why: Exhaustive search shows all three panels' extracted labels are feasible as the M-SQE series averaged over the three retrievers with integer per-language/region counts summing precisely to Table 3's implied totals (General 217/282, Tool-Use 308/795, Cultural 143/156), and infeasible as any single-retriever series; the Tool-Use and Cultural labels are also infeasible as Retrieve-only averages, pinning the series attribution. E.g., the General panel admits the clean partition fr=12, hi=20, ja=19, ko=10, sw=16, zh=17 (sums to 94) reproducing all six labels and the exact total. Passing a consistency test this brittle is strong evidence against fabricated or decorative figure numbers.

strengths.title: Cross-artifact coherence across figures, tables, and prose
strengths.location: Fig 4 (p7), Fig 5 (p7), Fig 6 (p7), Table 2 (p5), Table 1/abstract (p1), Sec 5.1 (p4)
strengths.why: Fig 4's Top-3 value 68.2 equals Table 3's BM25 three-domain M-SQE mean (204.5/3=68.17); Fig 6's main-setting cell (Retrieve-only 59.6 -> M-SQE 68.2, +8.6pp) equals the Table 3-derived BM25 means exactly; Sec 4's router accuracy (98.5%) matches Fig 5's "1.5% error rate" star; Table 2's layer sums check (400+550+800=1750; 1254+660+385=2299; 3384+1283+618=5285) and candidate depths follow the stated rule K=10*floor(|S|/1000) -> 10/20/50; the abstract's "~84,700" audit total matches Table 1's column sum (84,680); and Sec 5.1's quoted Prompt-only anchors (53.2/20.4/46.2) match Table 3 and imply integer counts (50/94, 54/265, 24/52).

strengths.title: Ablation claim verified and honestly framed
strengths.why: "M-SQE beats both single views on all three domains" checks out (74.5>71.3>67.0; 39.6>38.5>28.7; 90.4>88.5>59.6), and rather than overselling the fusion, the text volunteers that the gaps are "visibly uneven" — the Action view carries most of the gain (M-SQE is only +1.1 to +3.2 over Action-only) — and explains why. Reporting a result that partially deflates the framework's own two-view story is a credibility marker.

strengths.title: Table 5's numbers are internally honest even where the prose overreaches
strengths.why: All twelve cells are consistent with integer counts over 94/265/52 (e.g., 12.08=32/265, 42.31=22/52, 35.11=33/94), the M-SQE-vs-Retrieve-only tie at 50.00 in Cultural is printed rather than obscured, and the table includes both a Base (untrained) and a Random anchor, letting a reader see that skill-conditioned fine-tuning beats the untrained base in every column. The defect (see findings) is in the prose interpretation, not in the reported data.

strengths.title: Falsifiable experimental-design claims that could be checked, passed
strengths.why: The claim that the skill-necessity filter "leaves the Prompt-only anchor well below ceiling in all three domains (General 53.2%, Tool-Use 20.4%, and Cultural 46.2%)" is verifiable against Table 3 and correct, and Prompt-only is indeed the weakest row (39.9 avg), consistent with the paper's premise that the tasks require skills rather than parametric memory.

strengths.title: Table 3's Avg column is fully reproducible, including a subtle case proving unrounded aggregation
strengths.why: All ten row averages recompute from the nine cells to within rounding, and the one apparent mismatch is actually evidence of care: M-DaQ's naive average of printed cells is 53.556 (would print 53.6), but averaging the exact integer-count fractions (62/94, 56/94, 58/94, 81/265, 84/265, 91/265, 33/52, 30/52, 40/52) gives 53.546, matching the printed 53.5 — the Avg column was computed from unrounded values. The quoted deltas all verify exactly: 69.12-65.61=+3.5 vs SkillFlow, 69.12-62.82=+6.3 vs Retrieve-only, 69.12-55.14=+14.0 vs Random.

strengths.title: Near-universal integer consistency of reported percentages with the stated task counts
strengths.why: Every one of the 24 non-Random deterministic cells in Table 3, all 9 cells of Table 4, and all 12 cells of Table 5 is exactly k/n for the stated denominators (e.g., 39.6=105/265, 94.2=49/52, 38.30=36/94, 12.08=32/265). This is strong evidence that the stated task counts are the real denominators of the main tables and results are honestly reported at task granularity; fabricated or carelessly transcribed numbers rarely survive this test 45 times in a row.

strengths.title: Cross-figure and cross-table consistency checks all pass
strengths.location: Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6 (p.7) vs Table 3 (p.6) and Sec. 5.1 (p.4)
strengths.why: Fig. 4's Top-3 value 68.2 equals Table 3's M-SQE BM25 three-domain average (204.5/3=68.17); Fig. 6's main-setting cell (59.6 / 68.2) matches Retrieve-only and M-SQE BM25 averages; Fig. 5's low band around 50-51 matches the Random BM25 three-domain average 50.77 from Table 3; Fig. 5's 1.5%-error star matches the 98.5% router accuracy (6/411); the Prompt-only anchors quoted in Sec. 5.1 (53.2/20.4/46.2) match Table 3 exactly; and SkillFlow-as-selector on the SkillFlow retriever reproduces Retrieve-only(SF) identically (74.5/37.4/90.4) — exactly the idempotence one should see, an unforced internal sanity check that passes.

strengths.title: Setup arithmetic is exact: pool compositions, depth rule, and audit total
strengths.why: All three-layer pool sums are correct (400+550+800=1,750; 1,254+660+385=2,299; 3,384+1,283+618=5,285); the stated depth rule reproduces all three candidate depths (10/20/50); Table 1's per-language estimates sum to 84,680, consistent with the '~84,700' total; and N<=K holds for every reported budget.

strengths.title: Claim wording is calibrated to what the numbers actually show
strengths.why: 'First or tied-first' is verified accurate (two exact ties exist and the wording covers them); 'strictly ahead of both selection anchors in all 9 settings' verifies cell-by-cell; Fig. 6's '+3.5-9.0pp' range matches the six printed deltas; and the routing discussion honestly concedes the router's modest contribution ('routing sharpens the margin, and the two views hold the floor'), which matches the Table 4 arithmetic (Action-only alone is +6.5pp over Retrieve-only).

strengths.title: The router corruption sweep is the one place uncertainty is quantified, and it is done properly
strengths.why: 1,000 seeds per corruption rate with an empirical 95% band is a real stress test with real error bars, run on the component most open to a brittleness objection; the monotone degradation from +8.1pp at 10% to +4.5pp at 90% is internally coherent with the 0%-corruption margin of 8.6pp computable from Table 3.

strengths.title: Arithmetic and cross-figure consistency survives full recomputation
strengths.why: Every number I recomputed checks out: Table 3 row averages (M-SQE 69.1, SkillFlow 65.6, Retrieve-only 62.8, Random 55.1) reproduce the claimed +3.5/+6.3/+14.0pp; every cell is consistent with integer successes over n=94/265/52; the BM25 three-domain averages (68.2 M-SQE, 59.6 Retrieve-only) reappear exactly as Fig 4's Top-3 point and Fig 6's main cell; pool sizes sum correctly (400+550+800=1,750; 1,254+660+385=2,299; 3,384+1,283+618=5,285) and K=10*floor(|S|/1000) reproduces 10/20/50; Table 1 sums to ~84,680 vs the stated ~84,700; the router's 98.5% accuracy matches Fig 5's 1.5%-error star; 'first or tied-first in all 9 settings' and 'strictly ahead of both anchors in all 9' both verify cell-by-cell. No prose-table contradiction found.

strengths.title: The scorer=solver self-consistency confound is directly probed and does not explain the gains
strengths.why: Off-diagonal (scorer != solver) cells exist and remain positive: Gemini scorer -> Qwen3.6-Plus solver +9.0pp; Qwen3.6-Plus scorer -> Gemini solver +6.4pp; +5.0pp on the resynthesized pool. Mixed cells are not systematically smaller than matched cells (+9.0 vs +8.6 same-model), so a scorer preferring skills its own model executes well cannot account for the effect within the two backbones tested. Rebuilding the MT and self-generated layers with a different, stronger LLM (Qwen3.6-Plus) also preserves positive gains (+3.5/+5.0pp), addressing the generation-artifact confound. Caveats: only two scorer models, both strong, and no scorer variation on the resynthesized pool — but the core control is real and passes.

strengths.title: The router-corruption sweep is an honest control that bounds the authors' own component
strengths.why: Randomly flipping router labels on up to 90% of queries, with 1,000 seeds per rate and empirical 95% intervals, both demonstrates robustness (M-SQE stays above Retrieve-only throughout) and transparently quantifies the router's ceiling contribution (~3.6pp between +8.1pp at 10% and +4.5pp at 90% corruption). Publishing a control that limits the importance of one's own framework component is rigorous practice.

strengths.title: Skill-necessity anchor and solver-side anonymization guard against two real confounds
strengths.why: The Prompt-only anchor (53.2/20.4/46.2, all far below M-SQE's results) verifies tasks require skills rather than solver parametric memory — the filter explicitly screens out tasks that 'saturate without any skill'. And the solver receives 'anonymized skill bodies... (provenance labels and source identifiers stripped), without any gold answer or checker metadata' (Sec 4.1), closing the channel where the solver could favor skills by layer or origin.

strengths.title: The headline comparison targets the strongest, most relevant baseline under conditions favorable to it
strengths.why: The +3.5pp headline is computed against SkillFlow — the skill-specific state-of-the-art — whose ranking stage is additionally reused as a selector on top of every retriever, including its own full pipeline (the SF columns), and evaluation spans three retriever families (lexical, dense, skill-specific) so gains are not an artifact of one candidate distribution. Ties are reported as ties ('first or tied-first'), including the two cells where M-SQE only matches a baseline (Tool-Ne 36.2 = SkillFlow; Cultural-Ne 90.4 = mMARCO).

strengths.title: Budget sensitivity covers the deployment-relevant regime with a mechanistically coherent pattern
strengths.why: Testing N in {1,3,5,10} includes the small-context regime real agents occupy, and the margin over Retrieve-only widening as the budget tightens (+3.4pp at Top10 to +9.7pp at Top1) is exactly the signature a genuine selection-quality effect predicts, since larger budgets forgive individual bad picks; the Top-3 point (68.2) is consistent with Table 3.

strengths.title: The central motivational statistic (70.1% adoption, no gain) is verified genuine and correctly attributed
strengths.location: Sec 1 (p2, lines 99-102): "Even in English-only settings, Li et al. (2025) report that agents adopt a relevance-retrieved skill 70.1% of the time with no accompanying performance gain"; re-credited in Sec 4.3 (p3, lines 273-275)
strengths.why: I verified externally (arXiv:2504.06188 and its indexed abstract) that SkillFlow's Terminal-Bench analysis reports exactly this: a 70.1% skill use rate with no performance gain, attributed to the corpus lacking high-quality executable skills. The paper's most load-bearing motivational premise is accurately sourced, correctly quantified, and credited again where the Action view is designed to target it. The same check confirmed the citation's title and four-stage design match the paper's description ('faithfully reimplemented from its four-stage design').

strengths.title: The second motivational premise (curated skills help, self-generated can hurt) is a fair paraphrase of a verified source
strengths.location: Sec 1 (p2, lines 93-95) and Sec 3 (p2, lines 173-176): "Li et al. (2026) show that curated skills raise agent task success while self-generated ones offer little or even negative benefit"
strengths.why: Verified against SkillsBench (arXiv:2602.12670): curated Skills raise average pass rate by 16.2pp with negative deltas on a subset of tasks, and self-generated Skills provide no benefit on average. 'Offer little or even negative benefit' is a faithful, non-inflated paraphrase. Both of the paper's key empirical premises therefore rest on accurately reported prior findings, not on stretched citations.

strengths.title: Honest lineage disclosure and adversarial reuse of the closest competitor
strengths.location: Sec 4.2 (p3, lines 243-245): "These dimensions are inspired by existing multilingual instruction-data quality taxonomy (Liu et al. 2026c), and are further extended to the demands of multilingual agent skills"; Sec 5.3 (p5, lines 475-478, 494-496)
strengths.why: The paper does not claim its quality taxonomy from scratch - it names MIDB as the basis and identifies exactly which dimensions are new (executability, context efficiency, and the Action-view dimensions). It also names SkillFlow as 'the state-of-the-art skill-specific retrieval pipeline', reimplements it both as a retriever and as a post-retrieval selector baseline, and M-SQE is evaluated on top of SkillFlow's own retrieval. Positioning against the strongest prior system by running it, rather than omitting it, is good practice.

strengths.title: The two-family baseline design operationalizes the positioning claim empirically
strengths.location: Sec 3 'Positioning M-SQE' (p3, lines 200-210) mirrored in Sec 5.3 baselines and Table 3 (pp5-6)
strengths.why: The two gaps claimed in Sec 3 (relevance-only skill retrieval; static-only data quality) map one-to-one onto the two baseline families actually run: relevance rerankers (ToolRerank, SkillFlow's ranking stage, mMARCO) and quality scorers (DEITA, M-DaQ, JQL), each repurposed as post-retrieval selectors on identical candidate sets. The positioning is thus tested rather than merely asserted - Table 3 shows both families individually underperform the combination, which is the paper's structural claim. The one family missing is the prompted-LLM reranker (see findings), but what is claimed in Sec 3 is backed by an experiment.

strengths.title: Two genuinely novel artifacts: the multilingual skill-supply audit and the three-layer mixed-provenance pool design
strengths.location: Table 1 (p1, lines 49-59: en ~79,700 ... sw 0, hi 0 of ~84,700 entries); Sec 5.2 and Table 2 (pp4-5: 'ecological-style 400 + MT 550 + self-generated 800' etc.)

My overall verdict for this dimension: the scoring/fusion machinery is standard technique; the rubric content, the setting, the audit, and the pool construction are real contributions - this is a 'standard mechanism, new setting, novel evaluation artifacts, strong execution' paper, which is a legitimate and useful kind of paper, provided the mechanism-level framing is corrected.
